<summary>This page contains text from the first chapter of the Book of Esther, describing Queen Vashti's refusal to appear before King Ahasuerus and the subsequent legal counsel provided by Memucan. The manuscript includes marginal Masoretic notes and interlinear Judeo-Persian glosses that explain or translate specific Hebrew terms.</summary>
<keywords>Book of Esther, Ahasuerus, Vashti, Memucan, Persia, Media, Jewish law, Judeo-Persian, biblical manuscript, Masorah</keywords>

->The Book of Brilliance<-

What is this "Eighth" that you mentioned? Through it, He gave him the eight. Through it, the eight were completed in the count, although in his activity, he is the "Seventh." And what is it? The Right Hand, the Left Hand, the Head, the Body <note>original: "Berit," referring to the organ of the covenant</note> which decides between them, and his mate who is his wife, as it is written: "and he shall cleave to his wife." This makes eight. The eight days of circumcision correspond to these. But these are not eight, for the body and the covenant are one! Thus it is eight <note>likely counting the seven Sephirot plus the bride/Shekhinah</note>.

What is the Ninth? He said to him: The ninth is the "Upright Ones" <note>original: "Yesharim"</note> who unify this with that. One is higher than its fellow by five hundred years. They are like two wheels <note>Ofanim</note>. One inclines toward the side of the North, and the other inclines toward the side of the West, and they go down to the Bottom Earth. What is the "bottom"? It is the last of the lands below, the end of the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss> of the Holy One, blessed be He, which is under His feet, as it is written: "The heavens are My throne and the earth is My footstool." There is the victory of the world below, as it says "for ever and ever" <note>original: "Netzach Netzachim," suggesting Victory of Victories</note>. What is "forever and ever"? There is one "Victory" <note>Netzach</note>. What is the "Victory" that inclines to the West? And what is the second? The one that inclines to the North. And the third? That is the bottom-most. You said there are two wheels of the Chariot? Rather, say: the end of the <term>Shekhinah</term> is also called "Victory." Thus "for ever and ever"—one Victory and "Victories" which is two, making three.

His students said to him: From above to below we know, but from below to above we do not know. He said to them: Is it not the same from below to above, and above from the man? To Moses, the Rabbis said: Is it not a wall that goes up or down? For one who goes down, goes down quickly, but one who goes up does not. Furthermore, one who goes up can go up by another path so that he does not [have to] go down. He said to them: Go out! And he sat and expounded to them: Just as the <term>Shekhinah</term> is above, so it is below. And what is this <term>Shekhinah</term>? It is the light emanated from the first Light, which is Wisdom. It also contains everything, as it is written: "The whole earth is full of His glory." What is its function here? This is like a king who had seven sons and assigned each one his place. He said to them: Sit here, though I am far from you. He said to him: I am within you and see you all day. This is "The whole earth is full of His glory." Why is He among them? In order to establish them and sustain them.

And who are the sons? I have already told you: there are seven holy forms for the Holy One, blessed be He, and all of them correspond to man, as it is written: "For in the image of God He made man." These are: the Right Leg and the Left, the Right Hand and the Left, the Body, and the Covenant—that makes six. But it is written: "And He took one of his ribs." Was a "rib" taken? Yes, as you say, "and for the rib <note>side</note> of the Tabernacle," which we translate as "for the side of the Tabernacle." And what "side" <note>original: "setar"</note> is in it?

This is like a king who decided in his heart to plant nine male trees, and all of them were palm trees. He said: Since they are all of one kind, they will not endure. What did he do? He planted an <term>Etrog</term> <gloss>Citron</gloss> among them. It was one of those nine that arose in his thought to be males. And what is the <term>Etrog</term>? It is female. This is what is written: "The fruit of a majestic tree" <note>Hadar</note>, which we translate as "the fruit of the Etrog tree and palm branches." What is <term>Hadar</term> <gloss>Majesty/Beauty</gloss>? It is the beauty of everything. This is the beauty of the Song of Songs, of which it says: "Who is she that looks forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, awesome as an army with banners?" This is the name of the female, and it is in her name that she was taken from man, for it is impossible for the lower world to exist without the female.

And why is she called female <note>Nekevah</note>? After the name of the "openings" <note>Nekavim</note>, for her openings are wider and she has more openings than the man. And what are they? The breasts, the womb, and the place of reception. And what is the Song of Songs that you mentioned as "majesty"? Yes, it is the majesty of all, of all the holy fruits. For Rabbi Yohanan said: All the books [of the Bible] and all the Torah are holy, but the Song of Songs is the Holy of Holies. And what is "Holy of Holies"? It means it is holy to the holy ones. And who are the holy ones? Those who are in the form of man. And "Holy" refers to the "Majesty" <note>Hadar</note>, which is called by the name "Majesty." Do not read it as <term>Hadar</term> but as <term>Ha-dar</term> <gloss>The one who dwells</gloss>. This is the <term>Etrog</term>, which is separate from the binding of the <term>Lulav</term> <gloss>Palm branch</gloss>; the commandment of the Lulav is not fulfilled without it. Yet it is also bound with everything, for it is with every single one, and all of them are one. The Lulav corresponds to the spinal cord. And so he says: "And branches of thick trees"—it must be that its branches cover the ground.

What is this that you said, "the eighth"? In it, you provided the eight, and through it, the eight were completed for the count, but in its activity, it is the seventh. And what are these? The right hand and the left hand, and its head is the <term>brit</term> <gloss>covenant/circumcision</gloss> which acts as the arbiter, and its partner, which is its wife, as it is written: "and he shall cleave to his wife" (Gen. 2:24). Thus, it is eight, and the eight days of circumcision correspond to them. But if these eight were not there, the body and the covenant would be one, so it is eight. What is the ninth? He said to him: The ninth and the straight one that unites are one opposite the other, and one is higher than its fellow by five hundred years. They are like two wheels, and one inclines toward the north, and one inclines toward the west, and they descend to the lower earth. And what is the "lower"? It is the last of these lands below, and the end of the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss> of the Holy One, blessed be He, is beneath His feet, as it is said: "The heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool" (Isa. 66:1). And there is the victory of the world below, the two <term>netzach netzachaim</term> <gloss>eternity of eternities</gloss>. What is "to the eternity of eternities"? It is but one <term>netzach</term> <gloss>eternity/victory</gloss>. And what is this <term>netzach</term>? The one that inclines to the west. And the second to it, what is it? This is the one that inclines toward the north. And the third? This is the one below, the third. You spoke of two wheels of the chariot, so say instead that the end of the <term>Shekhinah</term> is also <term>netzach</term>. And this is "to the eternity of eternities," one <term>netzach</term> and two <term>netzachaim</term>, thus three. His students said to him: From above to below we understand, but from below to above we do not understand. He said to them: Is there not [a path] from below to above and from above to the <term>Adam</term> <gloss>Man</gloss>? The Sages said to Moses: It is not a wall that rises for the one descending, for the one descending descends in haste, while the one ascending is not so. Furthermore, the one ascending can ascend by another path so as not to descend. He said to them: Go out, and this one sat and lectured to them in the Name, that just as the <term>Shekhinah</term> is above, so it is below. And what is this <term>Shekhinah</term>? You might say this is the light emanated from the first light, which is wisdom. And it is also written of everything, as it is said: "The whole earth is full of His glory" (Isa. 6:3). What is its function here? A parable of a king who had seven sons and placed each in his own place. He said to them: Sit, each of you, at a distance from me. He said to him: I am written <note>or "present"</note> and see you all the day, and this is "The whole earth is full of His glory." And why is He among them? In order to sustain them and maintain them. And what are the sons? I have already told you, there are seven holy forms that the Holy One, blessed be He, has, and all of them correspond to <term>Adam</term>, as it is said: "For in the image of God He made the <term>Adam</term>" (Gen. 9:6). And these are: the right leg and the left, the right hand and the left, the <term>brit</term>, and there are six. And as it is written: "And He took one of his ribs" (Gen. 2:21). It was taken as it is written: "And He took one of his ribs." Does it have a side? Yes, as you say: "And for the side of the tabernacle" (Ex. 26:20), and we translate: "And for the side <term>setar</term> of the tabernacle." And what is <term>setar</term> in it? A parable of a king to whose heart it occurred to plant nine male trees, and they were all palms. He said: Since they are all from one source, they will not endure. What did he do? He planted an <term>etrog</term> <gloss>citron</gloss> among them, and it was one of those nine that arose in his thought to be male, and the <term>etrog</term>, what is it? A female. And this is what is written: "Fruit of a beautiful tree" (Lev. 23:40), and we translate: "Fruit of the tree, <term>etrogim</term> and palm branches." What is <term>hadar</term> <gloss>beauty/splendor</gloss>? It is the <term>hadar</term> of everything, and it is the <term>hadar</term> of the <term>Shir HaShirim</term> <gloss>Song of Songs</gloss>, of which it is said: "Who is she that looks forth like the dawn, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, terrible as an army with banners?" (Song 6:10). And this is by the name of the female, and by her name it was taken from <term>Adam</term>, for it is impossible that the lower world be empty without a female. And what is the reason? She is called female <note>in Hebrew, <term>nekebah</term></note> by the name of the openings, for she is wide and has more openings than the man. And what are they? The womb and the birth canal. And what is the <term>Shir HaShirim</term> that you said is <term>hadar</term>? It is the <term>hadar</term> of all, of all the holy books. For Rabbi Yochanan said: All the books and all the Torah are holy, and the <term>Shir HaShirim</term> is the holy of holies. And what is the holy of holies? It is that it is holy to the holy things. And what are the holy things? They are those that are in the form of <term>Adam</term>, and it is holy, for it is <term>hadar</term>, and its name is called <term>Hadar</term>. Do not read it <term>Hadar</term> but <term>Hadar</term> <note>a play on words connecting the citron to majesty</note>. This is the <term>etrog</term> separated from the bundle of the <term>lulav</term> <gloss>palm branch</gloss>, and the commandment of the <term>lulav</term> is not fulfilled except with it, and it is also bundled with everything, for with each and every one it is, and all of them together it is. The <term>lulav</term> corresponds to the spine, and so it says: "And branches of thick trees" (Lev. 23:40), it needs to be branches that cover the earth.

What is this that you said, "the eighth"? In it you placed the eight, and in it the eight are completed for the count, but in its activity, it is the seventh. And what are these? The right hand and the left hand, and its head, the <term>brit</term> <gloss>covenant/circumcision</gloss>, is the arbiter, and its partner, which is his wife, as it is written, "And he shall cleave unto his wife," and it becomes eight. And the eight days of circumcision correspond to them. And these eight do not exist <note>as distinct entities</note>, for the body and the covenant are one, and it is eight. What is the ninth? He said to him: The ninth and the straightforward <note>or "upright"</note> that unifies these against those, and one is higher than the other by five hundred years. They are like two <term>ofanim</term> <gloss>wheels/angels</gloss>, and one leans to the north and one leans to the west, and they descend to the lower earth. And what is the "lower"? The last of these lands below, and the end of the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss> of the Holy One, blessed be He, is beneath His feet, as it is said, "The heavens are My throne, and the earth is the footstool of My feet." And there is the victory of the world below: the second "victory of victories." What is "to the victory of victories"? It is but one victory. And what is the one that leans to the west, and what is the second to it? This is the one that leans toward the north, and the third is this, the lower one below. You said there were two wheels of the chariot, so say instead that the end of the <term>Shekhinah</term> is also victory. And this is "to the victory of victories": one victory, two victories, behold three. His students said to him: From above to below we understand, but from below to above we do not understand. He said to them: And does it not exist from below to above, and from above the person? They said to the masters regarding Moses: It is not a wall that rises to one who descends, for one who descends, descends in a rush, and one who ascends is not like this. And furthermore, the one who ascends can ascend by another path, so that he does not descend. He said to them: Go and sit. And he taught them in the name that as the <term>Shekhinah</term> is above, so it is below. And what is this <term>Shekhinah</term>? You might say this is the light emanated from the first light, which is wisdom. And it is also written of everything, as it is said, "The whole earth is full of His glory." What is its work here? # Mawlana Ubayd Zakani

## ( The Preferred School )

When the great ones and the subtle, keen-minded thinkers who now honor the face of the earth with their noble presence reflected upon the perfection of the human spirit and its return and afterlife, and kept before their eyes the traditions and opinions of former elites, they developed a complete denial of those beliefs. They say that it has been revealed to us that the rational soul has no independent standing; its permanence is tied to the permanence of the body, and its annihilation is dependent on the annihilation of the physical frame. They say that what the prophets stated regarding its having perfection or deficiency, and that it will remain self-subsisting after parting from the body, is impossible, and the Resurrection and Judgment are false matters. Life consists only of the balance of the body's composition; once the body decomposes, that person becomes nothing and void forever. Whatever is described as the pleasures of paradise or the punishment of hell can also exist in this world, as the poet said:

-> ( Verse ) <-

> To the one who was meant to receive it, they gave it right here
> And for the one who has nothing, they promised it for tomorrow

Naturally, they are completely free from the concerns of Resurrection, Judgment, punishment, torment, proximity to God, distance from God, divine pleasure, or wrath, and perfection or deficiency. The result of this belief is that they spend every day of their lives in the pursuit of desires and the attainment of pleasures, saying:

-> ( Quatrain ) <-

> O you who are the result of the four and seven <note>the four elements and seven planets</note>
> And are constantly in distress because of these seven and four
> Drink wine, for I have told you a thousand times
> There is no coming back for you; once you are gone, you are gone

And they write most of this quatrain on the headstones of their fathers' graves:

-> ( Quatrain ) <-

> Beyond this ceiling, there is no portico or hallway
> Except for me and you, there is no intellect or discernment
> That "nothing" which the imagination thought was "something"
> Pass happily from this fancy, for that "something" is nothing

And it is because of this belief that the intent to shed blood, take property, or harm the honor of people seems trivial and insignificant to them.

-> ( Verse ) <-

> To him, one gulp of wine the color of fire
> Is more precious than the blood of a hundred brothers

THE STORY OF SAṄKHA.

1. Again, when I was a brahmin named Saṅkha, I wished to cross the great ocean and approached the harbor.
2. There, on the path, I saw the Self-Existent <note>referring to a Buddha</note>, the Unconquered One, who had embarked upon a journey through a wilderness, traveling across difficult, rugged ground.
3. Having seen Him on the path, I reflected on this matter: "This is a fertile field <note>a metaphor for an opportunity to perform a virtuous deed</note> for a person desiring merit."
4. Just as a farmer, having seen a large field, does not plant seeds there if he does not care for grain;
5. So too, if I, desiring merit, having seen the most excellent field, do not perform a deed there, then I do not care for merit.
6. Just as a minister, desiring a reward, does not give wealth and grain to the people in the king’s inner palace, he loses his reward.
7. So too, if I, desiring merit, having seen a vast field for offering, do not give a gift to Him, I shall fall away from merit.
8. Having thought this, I descended, took off my sandals, worshipped His feet, and gave Him the pair of sandals.
9. Because of that, I have been delicate and established in happiness a hundred times over; and furthermore, fulfilling the practice of giving <term>dâna</term> <gloss>generosity/almsgiving</gloss>, I gave them to Him in this way.

II.

### THE STORY OF SANKHA

1. Again, when I was a Brahman named Sankha <note>original: Saṅkhasavhayo</note>, wishing to cross the great ocean, I arrived at a seaport.

2. There, on the road, I saw a Self-Existent One <note>original: sayambhum; referring to a Private Buddha or Paccekabuddha</note> who was unconquered by passions. He was walking along a desert path on the scorched and hardened ground.

3. Seeing him on the road, I reflected on this matter: This is a field of merit <note>original: khettam</note> arrived for a person desiring to perform good deeds.

4. Just as a farmer who sees a field of great potential but does not plant seeds there has no use for grain;

5. In the same way, I, who desire merit, have seen a supreme and excellent field. If I do not perform a service there, I have no desire for merit.

6. Just as an official who wishes for the king's favor <note>original: muddikâmo; literally desiring the seal or stamp of approval</note> but does not give wealth or grain to the people in the king's palace is deprived of that favor;

7. In the same way, I, who desire merit, have seen a person most worthy of gifts. If I do not give a gift to him, I will be deprived of merit.

8. Having thought this, I took off my sandals and, having paid homage at his feet, I gave him my sunshade and sandals.

9. Because of that deed, I became a hundred times more delicate and established in happiness. Thus, fulfilling the perfection of giving <note>original: dânam</note>, I gave that gift to him.

THE CONDUCT OF SANKHA, THE SECOND.

Against the evil of the enemy, I am a shield.
The tip of my sword is at the throat of the soul,
From this end, I am joyful and victorious.
My form is one, yet I move with haste,
I strike the head of the father of delay.
Seek until my third breath,
With one hand, my body is a single burning flame.
I am the sustenance of friends in this new land.

<column-break/>

When the king placed his foot upon the golden throne,
The head of one like me rose from the dust of humility.
In a place where my work is settled,
I shall give justice to the oppressed.
I take the path of righteousness today,
Before the forehead of the elephant and the foot of the ant.
From the grace of the Sun of the afterworld,
If I find a treasure from the world, it is through wisdom.
I bring the head of the wise to greatness,
When anyone enters the path of knowledge.
In every night of hope, I have a share,
I have no fear of any thorn or hardship.
I cast down the head of those who seek rest,
In place of one, I shall do for one.
When the neck-stretching pride of anger appears,
I endure the pain that fills the throat.
To me, it is like a mule in the pasture,
From that breath, this head is better off.
With a firm foot, I have melted away the dross,
By that Truth which we have known from of old.

<column-break/>

From the treasure of speech, beauty and excellence come forth,
I take my place like one who is newly purified.
Because I was born such, I shall act thus,
Make haste, for I shall act with a pure nature.
So that I may inform you of the way ahead,
It does not come from me to act as others do.
I do not wish to cause pain to anyone,
For the one who is drunk is the one who is lost.
I bind the feet of the madman,
I wish to be free from the stain of shame.
In my own vengeance, I am like a name,
Except for the one who is a stone in the path.
I open the door that must be opened,
In the place of goodness, I shall do a hundredfold.
When I am not alone in my enmity,
I take back and pour out again in its place.
The head of need is what I abandon,
For I have become the helper of the fallen.
I have killed oppression with its own point,
From me, the messenger’s bond is made whole.

### Regulation for Chachar Land ###

When land falls out of use due to heavy rains or floods, the farmers suffer hardship in its restoration. In the first year, they take two parts out of five; in the second, three; in the third, four; and in the fifth, they take the full standard rate. Depending on the place, cash or grain is demanded. In the third year, as requested, they add one <term>dam</term> to the ten and a half.

### Regulation for Banjar Land ###

When there is a great difference due to flooding, they demand revenue in this manner:
**Spring Harvest:** For wheat on flooded land, in the first year they take half a <term>man</term> per <term>Bigah</term>; the second year, one <term>man</term>; the third, two; the fourth, three.

Let it be known with certainty that whoever deviates from this will be addressed in the same manner as the judge. It has happened that since Arshad and Qassar were both free men, they were reproached in the most severe and humiliating manner, for if the intellect, integrity, and order of the affairs of the scholars are maintained, and we are determined to spend the effort in acquiring and perfecting the means for this, then several necessary meanings—which have been acquired from the honor of the intellect and the signing of the effects of the laws of the <term>Sharia</term>—have been verified with former judges, and we must make the necessity of following them understood to the judges of the provinces so that they may proceed according to that and avoid going beyond it.

<insert>First,</insert> that caution must be employed regarding the hearing of testimony so that it does not enter into the realm of the hidden; rather, when a preponderance of evidence regarding the essence and the truth of it is obtained, they shall rule on it and be content with that, lest the judge be helpless and at fault, and the catastrophe of it not be approved by the people, and it happens that the case itself is dangerous. Since the good character is known and caution has been exercised, they pass a judgment in it, and the people—being supported by those with wealth and influence—become <note>original: "واسطه مسا صل"</note>, and the secret of this meaning is lost upon us. Although the <term>Sharia</term> requires two witnesses and stipulates the condition of justice, and justice is a great matter that rarely manifests except in select individuals, the judge must think deeply that perhaps the testimony is being given based on passion, or in league with the person who is the perpetrator of a crime, or that the witness—by merely displaying the appearance and conduct of a righteous man—deceives the judge into accepting the testimony. One must employ the work to clarify the true state of affairs and remove ambiguity and confusion. And since <note>a reference to Ali ibn Abi Talib</note> said that whatever is hidden in the heart is revealed upon one's tongue, and that which is hidden in the concealment of the soul can be found by its owner, we have commanded that in the hearing of any testimony that causes doubt in the mind, they shall proceed with caution. Whoever reaches a state of certainty through those witnesses, and the state of their justice is determined, and whoever is clear in the phrasing of affairs, and whoever comes to the local assemblies repeatedly, let them investigate the circumstances from the additions of the location. And the questions that are in the state of inquiry—such as the exposing of times and places, the words of the contract, the circumstances of the case, and the nature of the questions—that have a bearing on the truth of those matters, they must exercise <term>ijtihad</term> <gloss>independent legal reasoning</gloss> so that the desired truth may appear, with such soundness that one can pass a judgment on it that is based on the truth, preventing the judge from falling into the abyss of a false ruling. And since the flaws that occur in judgment happen because of the certification of the witnesses <note>original: "ترکیه مزکان"</note>, which is not done with enough precision, one must be cautious in that category of testimony, and for the <term>fazl</term> <gloss>virtue/superiority</gloss> that is upon the path of excellence in the matter of certification, one must consider the foundation to be binding. 

<insert>Another:</insert> They have employed deliberation and patience in the matter of the rulings [documents] that they seal, for there is much ambiguity in that category. Most judges, who have established themselves in their regions and districts, leave the <term>wilayat</term> <gloss>jurisdiction</gloss> to the possession of the local notables, and those who are informed about the secrets of that region and the causes of that case, and the validity and hearing of it depend upon those notables. They send the unsigned documents to other judges, or they bring them, and they pass a ruling on its truth, and thus falsehood takes on the appearance of truth. The way to salvation from this abyss is that the judges, by inquiring into the state of the case and the necessity of its occurrence, must be informed and gain full understanding, and they must not hasten to open and judge.

<insert>Another:</insert> Caution in matters that relate to <term>hajj</term> <gloss>pilgrimage</gloss>, legal documents, various types of books, and classes of rulings that have <term>mujalat</term> <gloss>journals/registers</gloss>, for if one writes from ignorance, it will be empty of virtue, and the amount that the events of the seals entail leads to the invalidation of rights, and that flaw lies with some of the scribes. Regarding the requirements and conditions of the scribe, regarding the devotion of the heart and the guarding of the soul, and since a general remedy was necessary for the faults, we commanded a group of notables and people of action who were famous for the precision of their vision to assemble with us.

Our concern and attention to the administration of affairs in the text is for the sake of benefit, and if ease and negligence in the affairs of the <term>Shar'</term> <gloss>Islamic Law</gloss> should arise, firmness and steadfastness in their proper place would become possible. It should be realized that whoever deviates from this will be addressed in the same manner as the judge of the court. Often, when both the superior and the minor are free men, they have been rebuked in the most intimidating and severe manner. If the intellect, integrity, and organization of the affairs of the scholars are maintained, and we devote ourselves to the study and mastery of their causes, we will have verified several necessary meanings with the previous rulers, derived from the honor of the intellect and the implementation of the traces of the laws of the <term>Shar'</term>. We bring to the understanding of the judges of the realms the necessity of following them, so that they may proceed accordingly and not transgress them.

<insert>First</insert>, that caution in the matter of hearing testimony should enter into the hidden aspects of the situation. When the preponderance of opinion is obtained in its true nature, they should judge by it. They should know that if a judge is incapable or sinful, the people will not approve of the consequence, and it happens that the case itself is dangerous. Since they have known the good condition and have exercised caution, they pass a judgment, and the people, relying on the wealthy master, become involved. This meaning escapes them: although the <term>Shar'</term> has made testimony contingent upon two witnesses and has conditioned it upon justice, and justice is a great matter that rarely manifests except in individuals, the soul's desire, if the creation is irresponsible, must be carefully considered by the ruler. He might testify against someone out of personal desire, or for the sake of a criminal, and merely through that witness, he might adorn himself with the appearance of righteousness and deceive the judge. In the search for a good condition and the investigation of the hidden essence of the case, one must be diligent. It is appropriate to clarify the condition, and for ambiguity and doubt to be removed. When the judge investigates such matters, he reveals what is in the heart. The Commander of the Faithful, Ali (peace be upon him), said that whatever is hidden in the heart is confirmed by the tongue, and whatever is concealed in the hand of the oppressor, one can find from his secret. We have ordered that in hearing any testimony that causes doubt, they should act with caution. Whoever reaches the reliable witnesses, they should know the truth with their signatures. And as for those who are remiss in the style of affairs and the precision of words, and those who come to the courts, they should inquire about the circumstances. The questions that are in the inquiry, such as the time and place, the specific words, and the hidden aspects of the case which have a bearing on the truth of those matters, must be investigated with effort so that the truth is revealed and a judgment can be made that is beneficial to the people, or a caution that stops the path and saves them from the abyss of false judgment.

Since the flaws that occur in the judiciary are caused by the purification of the witnesses, which is not done with proper care, caution must be exercised in that category of testimony. And concerning the excellence that is required in the matter of certification based on the foundations of the <term>Shar'</term>, it is necessary.

<insert>Another</insert> point: they should be careful and hesitant in the matter of those who bring rulings and seal them, as many doubts arise in that category. Most of the judges who have set their own districts and regions allow the masters of those places to transmit the judgments. When they become informed of the events and causes of that case in that region, and the truth and hearing of it are covered by those judges, they must send it to another judge for verification, sealed and without bias. They should seek the truth of it and judge accordingly. Otherwise, the false is imagined to be true, and the path to salvation from this abyss is for the judges to become informed about the true nature of that case and the necessity of the reality of that situation before they send it. They should have full knowledge and not hasten in resolving and judging.

<insert>Another</insert> point: caution in matters relating to wills, documents, various books, and categories of rulings with their seals. If it is written by a scribe, it may be devoid of truth, and many sums of money result in the invalidation of rights due to the ignorance of the matters. That flaw lies with some writers, and the requirements and conditions for writing require devotion of heart and care. Since general rectification was necessary in the writing of documents, we have ordered a group of scholars and officials who were known for their precision of vision to accompany us and summarize them.

Distraction and lack of focus in managing affairs lead to losses in worldly matters and negligence in the practice of religious law. However, firmness, strength, and steadfastness in these matters make resolution possible. It is understood by those who investigate that anyone who deviates from this path will face the same admonition as a judge who acts unjustly. It is often the case that when men—both the senior and the common—are free individuals, they are rebuked in the harshest and most severe manner. If the intellect, integrity, and orderly conduct of the learned are to be supported, we must expend our efforts in securing and perfecting the means to achieve this. Several essential points regarding the dignity of the intellect and the implementation of the effects of legal statutes have been verified with former rulers, and we must ensure the judges of the realm understand the necessity of following them so that they proceed accordingly and do not transgress. 

<insert>First</insert>, caution must be exercised when hearing testimony. One must not rely solely on the prevalence of conjecture in the exterior appearance of the witness, for this leads to erroneous judgments and renders the judge incapable and sinful. The harm of such errors is not approved by the people, and it often happens that the case itself is perilous. When the judge, believing in the good character of the witnesses and having acted with caution, issues a ruling, and then it is discovered that the wealthy and influential parties were involved, the truth is lost. Although the religious law requires two witnesses and stipulates the condition of justice—a quality that is rare and seldom found in individuals—the judge must ponder deeply. He should consider that perhaps the testimony is motivated by personal desire or by one who holds a grudge against the defendant. The judge must not be deceived by the superficial appearance of the witnesses or the fact that they are respected men. Instead, he must investigate the truth of the matter and the sincerity of their inner state. 

It is said that one must clarify the circumstances to remove ambiguity and doubt. When a judge investigates these matters, the truth—no matter how deeply hidden—will eventually manifest. The Commander of the Faithful, Ali (peace be upon him), stated that whatever is hidden in the heart will be revealed by the tongue, and whatever is concealed in the heart of a person, one can eventually discover through their speech. We have ordered that in hearing any testimony where there is doubt, judges must exercise extreme caution. They should investigate the witnesses' history and character. Those assigned to these tasks must arrive at the truth by asking pertinent questions regarding times, places, specific words, and the underlying circumstances of the case. By posing deep questions that have a bearing on the matter, they will uncover the truth and avoid the pitfalls of false judgments. 

Since many of the flaws in judicial rulings stem from the validation of witnesses—where the judge does not exert himself to verify their character—extreme caution must be applied in that validation. The importance of verifying witnesses is a fundamental duty.

<insert>Second</insert>, deliberation and patience must be applied to rulings regarding documents that are sealed. Many doubts arise in these matters. Most judges who are assigned to their own districts receive these documents from other regions. Because they lack information regarding the local circumstances or the context of the case, they may rush to issue a ruling based on sealed documents sent by other judges. Consequently, falsehood may appear as truth. The way to escape this trap is for the judge to send an investigator to the site of the event to become fully informed and gain complete understanding before rushing to issue a judgment.

<insert>Third</insert>, caution is required in matters concerning deeds, legal documents, various records, and the categories of rulings and official letters. If a scribe writes incorrectly, the result is full of errors. Often, a small oversight in these documents leads to the nullification of rightful claims. This flaw lies with some scribes. Therefore, the requirements and conditions for scribes, such as care, vigilance, and precision, must be strictly observed. Since it is necessary to redress these errors, we have appointed a group of knowledgeable and diligent individuals, known for their sharp intellect, to supervise these matters.

No one has beauty like Baktash,
No one has the possibility of being more beautiful than him.

Since one can speak of that tall cypress,

Since his forehead is a field of silver,

# The Twenty-First Discourse

My heart has become my adversary; what shall I do? This musician cannot find the right melody for this mode.
Now I have become a wanderer of the horizons, for I have joined the ranks of those behind the veil of lovers.
When I heard a song from that rebellious beauty, I made a daily portion for that veil from my eyes <note>meaning he shed tears over the veil or musical mode</note>.
Her love brought me so much into myself that it brought a hundred years of sorrow before me.
Her tresses scattered my state of being in such a way that the kingdom of my gathered composure fell into decline.
The ring of her lock of hair tightened its belt so firmly that my heart turned to blood until it clotted like liver.
I am this ill and bewildered because I know that I do not know her true worth.
No one possesses beauty as Bektash <note>the male protagonist of the romance of Gul and Bektash</note> does, for it is not possible for anyone to be more beautiful than he.
Since one can speak of that cypress-like stature without words, why should one speak of anyone else?
Since her forehead is a field of silver, what fear have I if I make a polo-stick from her tresses?
In that field, with that polo-stick of her tresses, I wish to take the ball of her chin.
If she makes a polo-stick of her tresses, she makes my head turn like a ball.
If her face shines forth openly, every atom would become a hundred fragments of the moon.
When the crescent of her cheek cast its halo, it made the new moon wail in grief for her.
As her heart-stealing tress became ringed, a hundred souls were girded in every single ring.
The pupil of the eye found its blackness from her narcissus-eye; for that reason, it became a recluse in her assembly.
When the arrow of her glance took effect, the spear and javelin were girded in fear of her.
She has down on her lip by those thirty-piece teeth <note>a metaphor for teeth as white as the thirty sections of the Quran</note>; because of my blood, her lips are laughing.

### A Discourse on the Judgment and Strategy of Governing the Kingdom and Leading an Army

As long as the work can be accomplished through strategy,
Tolerance of the enemy is better than warfare.

When the enemy cannot be defeated by force,
One must close the door of sedition with wealth.

If there is fear of harm from your adversary,
Seal his tongue with the talisman of generosity.

Strew generosity in the place of caltrops <note>original: "خسک" (khask), a spiked device used to slow enemy movement</note> for the enemy,
For generosity makes the sharp tooth blunt.

When a hand cannot be bitten, kiss it;
For with the dominant, the remedy is deceit and flattery.

Through the strategy of <term>Rostam</term> <gloss>the legendary Persian hero</gloss>, one enters the bonds,
For <term>Esfandiyar</term> <gloss>a legendary warrior</gloss> did not seek him out from the lasso.

One can peel the skin off the enemy when there is an opportunity;
Then, treat him with such tolerance that he becomes a friend.

Beware of the battle of the smallest person,
For I have seen many floods from a single drop.

Do not frown if you can help it,
For a friend is better than an enemy, even if the enemy is weak.

His enemy is fresh and his friend is wounded;
Whoever has more enemies than friends.

Do not fight with an army greater than your own,
For one cannot strike with a lancet against a thumb.

It is a pity to share knowledge with the low-minded,
As seeds are wasted on barren soil.

Since they will not grasp it, they will view you as an enemy;
They will suffer in their soul and inflict suffering upon you.

Your habit, O King, is to face the truth;
The heart of a man who speaks truth is strong because of this.

A signet ring has a property, O fortunate one,
That it leaves an impression in wax, but not in hard stone.

It is no wonder if a tyrant is troubled by my presence,
For he is a thief and I am the watchman.

You, too, act as a watchman with justice and fairness,
So that God’s protection may be the watchman over you.

You owe no debt based on your own efforts;
Praise and grace belong to God alone,

Who kept you employed in acts of goodness,
And did not leave you idle like others.

Everyone is on the field of exertion,
But not everyone carries away the ball of generosity.

You did not earn paradise through your own effort;
God imbued your nature with heavenly qualities.

May your heart be bright and your time peaceful;
May your feet be firm and your status exalted.

May your life be pleasant and your departure correct;
May your worship be accepted and your prayers answered.

### Discourse on Counsel, Administration of the Kingdom, and Military Strategy

As long as matters can be resolved through strategy,
Tolerance of an enemy is better than open warfare.

When it is impossible to defeat an enemy by force,
One must close the door to sedition with wealth.

If there is fear of harm from your adversary,
Bind his tongue with the charm of kindness.

Instead of thorns, strew benefits in the enemy's path,
For kindness dulls the sharpest teeth.

When you cannot bite a hand, kiss it;
For when dealing with the powerful, the remedy is flattery and artifice.

Through strategy, even Rustam <note>A legendary Persian hero</note> can be captured;
He whom Isfandiyar <note>Another legendary hero, known for his invulnerability</note> could not catch with his lasso.

Once you have the opportunity to overwhelm an enemy,
Treat him with such courtesy that he becomes a friend.

Beware of fighting the humblest of people;
For I have often seen a flood originate from a mere drop.

Do not furrow your brow as long as you are able,
For it is better to have a friend, even if the enemy is weak.

He whose enemies outnumber his friends
Finds his enemies thrive while his friends wither.

Do not engage with an army larger than your own;
One cannot strike a lancet with a finger.

### Discourse on Counsel, Governance, and Military Command

As long as matters can be resolved through strategy, 
clemency toward an enemy is better than conflict.

When one cannot defeat an enemy through force,
one must close the door of sedition with generosity.

If you fear harm from your adversary,
tie his tongue with the amulet of kindness.

Instead of thorns, scatter kindness in the enemy's path,
for kindness blunts the sharpest of teeth.

When one cannot bite a hand, one must kiss it,
for when facing superiors, the remedy is flattery and artifice.

Through cunning, even a <term>Rostam</term> <gloss>the legendary Persian hero</gloss> can be captured;
<term>Esfandiyar</term> <gloss>a legendary hero known for his invulnerability</gloss> could not escape from the trap.

One can peel the skin off an enemy when the opportunity arises;
then, treat him with such courtesy that he becomes a friend.

Beware of warring with a person of lesser status,
for I have seen many a flood born from a single drop.

Do not knit your brows as long as you are able,
for even if an enemy is weak, a friend is better.

The one who has more enemies than friends,
finds his enemies flourishing while his friends are wounded.

Do not strike at an army larger than your own,
for one cannot strike a lancet with a finger.

If your words take no effect on him, he will consider you an enemy; he will be grieved in his soul and will seek to grieve you in return.

Your habit, O King, is toward the truth; for this reason, the heart of the truth-teller is made strong.

The signet ring has a quality, O fortunate one: it leaves its mark in wax, not in hard stone.

It is no wonder if the tyrant is vexed by me to his very soul, for he is a thief and I am the watchman.

You also are a watchman through equity and justice; may the protection of God be your watchman.

By right of logic, you have no claim of merit; rather, favor, grace, and thanks belong to the Lord,

Who employed you in His service for good works, and did not leave you idle like others.

All people are in the field of striving, but not everyone carries away the prize of bounty.

You did not attain Paradise through your own effort; God instilled a heavenly nature within you.

May your heart be enlightened and your time untroubled; may your step be firm and your rank exalted.

May your life be pleasant and your passing be righteous; may your worship be accepted and your prayers answered.

<column-break/>

### Discourse on Counsel, Statecraft, and Leading Armies

As long as a matter can be resolved through counsel, it is better to show forbearance to the enemy than to engage in battle.

When you cannot break the enemy by force, you must close the door of strife with riches <note>meaning bribery or generous gifts to pacify an opponent</note>.

If you fear harm from your adversary, bind his tongue with the amulet of kindness.

Scatter pearls in the path of the foe instead of caltrops <note>original: "khasak," spiked iron devices used to wound horses or soldiers</note>; for kindness blunts the sharpest teeth.

When you cannot bite a hand, kiss it; for with the powerful, the remedy is deception and flattery.

Even a hero like <term>Rustam</term> <gloss>the legendary champion of Persian epic</gloss> is caught in the snare of counsel, though <term>Esfandiyar</term> <gloss>the prince of the Shahnameh</gloss> could not catch him with a lasso.

When the opportunity arises, one can flay the skin of an enemy; until then, treat him with the kindness shown to a friend.

Beware of warring with even the least of men, for I have seen many a flood born from a single drop.

Do not knit your brow in anger as long as you are able; for even if the enemy is weak, a friend is better.

The one who has more enemies than friends will find his enemies refreshed and his friends wounded.

Do not strike at an army larger than your own; one cannot press a finger against a lancet.

His mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem. 

Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you? 

My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies. I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine; he who grazes among the lilies. 

You are beautiful, my love, as <term>Tirzah: an ancient royal city in the northern kingdom of Israel, celebrated for its aesthetic beauty</term>, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners. Turn away your eyes from me, for they have overcome me. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from <term>Gilead: a region east of the Jordan River known for its rich pastures</term>. Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and not one among them is bereaved. Your brow is like a slice of pomegranate behind your veil. 

There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and young women without number. My dove, my perfect one, is unique. She is the only one of her mother, pure to her who bore her. The daughters saw her and called her blessed; the queens and the concubines praised her. 

Who is she who looks forth like the dawn, fair as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as an army with banners? 

I went down to the nut orchard to look at the blossoms of the valley, to see whether the vine had budded and the pomegranates were in bloom. Before I was aware, my soul set me among the chariots of my noble people. 

Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you. Why should you look upon the Shulammite, as upon the dance of <term>Mahanaim: a Hebrew term meaning 'two camps', which may refer to a specific liturgical or celebratory dance</term>? 

How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O noble daughter! Your rounded thighs are like jewels, the work of a master’s hand. Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat, encircled with lilies. Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.

<column-break/>

Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are pools in <term>Heshbon: a city east of the Jordan known for its impressive water reservoirs</term>, by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like a tower of Lebanon, looking toward Damascus. Your head crowns you like <term>Carmel: a coastal mountain range in Israel famous for its lush greenery and fertility</term>, and your flowing locks are like purple; a king is held captive in the tresses. 

How beautiful and how pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights! This stature of yours is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like its clusters. I said, "I will climb the palm tree and lay hold of its fruit." May your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples. And your mouth is like the best wine that goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding over the lips of those who sleep. 

I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me. Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field; let us lodge in the villages. Let us go out early to the vineyards and see if the vine has budded, if the grape blossoms have opened and the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love. 

The <term>mandrakes: a plant with roots often shaped like humans, anciently associated with fertility and love</term> give forth fragrance, and at our doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you, my beloved. 

O that you were like a brother to me, who nursed at my mother’s breasts! If I found you outside, I would kiss you, and no one would despise me. I would lead you and bring you into the house of my mother; she would teach me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranates. 

His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me. 

I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that you do not stir up or awaken love until it pleases. 

Who is that coming up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved? Under the apple tree I awakened you. There your mother was in labor with you; there she who bore you was in labor.

# Crown of Kingdom

Woe, woe to me, for my inclination has snatched me, and my days are upheavals. Tomorrow, worms will cover me, the day of death will seize me, and the grave will hide me. What shall I answer, and what shall I say? If poor and hungry, he is pained for a piece of bread; if he pursues wealth, his feet are swift, and he forgets the day of death while in his rooms. In the time of distress, he multiplies his words, changes his speech, and increases his vows. In his pride, he divides his words like the sea, sends forth his hands, and reinforces the bars of his gates, yet death is at his door. He multiplies guards on every side, while the ambush sits in the room; the ambush does not stop him. A siege wall came against the flock, and he knew not why. He rejoices, and knows not in what. He lives, and knows not for how long. In his days, he walks in his ways, and when his sickness begins, suddenly he awakens to seek force and wealth. He departs from his place to ride ships, to tread on dry land, and to bring his soul into the dens of lions. He tosses among the beasts, and in his darkness, because his glory is great and his hand has found much, the destroyer comes upon him. His eye is open, and he is gone. At all times, he is prepared for the miseries of illnesses and signs, and at all hours, for accidents. If he tires, he stands in peace; suddenly, disaster comes upon him. In every moment, there are encounters, and in every day, threats are upon him. If he enters into war, the sword will overtake him, or a bow of bronze will replace him; or griefs will surround him, or surging waters will wash him away, or a bad and bitter illness will change him until he becomes a burden upon his own soul, and he drains the bitterness of his cup to the dregs. In his old age, his suffering grows, he weakens, the young mock him, children rule over him, and he becomes a burden to those who came from his own loins. All his acquaintances act like strangers to him, and when his time comes, he leaves his chambers for the court of death, from the shadow of his rooms to the shadow of death. He casts off his embroidery, wears worms, and worms will clothe him; he will return to the dust. He returns to his foundation from which he was hewn. For a man such as this, when will he find a time for repentance to scrub away the filth of apostasy? The day is short, the work is great, the taskmasters are urgent, hasty, and running, and time mocks him, while the Master of the house presses. Therefore, I pray, my God, remember these miseries that come upon man. And if I have done evil, You shall do good; do not repay measure for measure to a man whom flesh has afflicted, and who has been ensnared by his iniquities without desire. My God, if my iniquity is too great to bear, what will You do for Your great name? <margin>And if I have sinned against You, it is a desecration.</margin> To Your arm, who can spare me except You? Therefore, if You slay me, I will hope in You; if You seek out my iniquity, I will flee from You to You, and cover myself from Your wrath in Your shadow. I will hold onto the hem of Your garment until You have had mercy on me, and I will not let You go unless You bless me. Remember, I pray, that You made me like clay, and in these miseries, You have tested me. Therefore, do not visit upon me according to my deeds, and do not make me eat the fruit of my actions. Prolong my time, and do not hasten my days until I have prepared provisions to return to my place. Do not press me to hurry to be sent from the earth, and do not place the burdens of the earth upon my shoulders. And when You weigh my iniquities, place my miseries in the second scale, and in the furnace of my affliction...

# Crown of Sovereignty

Woe, woe unto me, for my impulse is a predator, and my days are an upheaval. A day of maggots awaits tomorrow, and the day of death shall seize me, and the grave shall hide me. What shall I answer, and what shall I say? Woe, and hunger for a crust of bread causes pain. The seeker of wealth, his feet are swift, and he forgets the day of death while he is in his chambers. At the time of distress, he increases his utterances, changes his words, and multiplies his vows; but in his expanse, he divides his words, stretches out his hands, and bolsters the bolts of his gates—yet death is in his courtyards. He increases guards on every side, but the lurker sits in the room, and no wall can restrain the lurker. The siege comes against the herd, and he does not know why; he rejoices, and he does not know for what; he lives, yet he does not know for how long. He walks in his ways during his days, and when his illness begins, suddenly, all at once, he awakens to seek wealth and fortune. He travels from his place to ride on ships, to tread on dry lands, and to bring his soul into the dens of lions. At every moment, there are afflictions; on every day, there are threats. the beating of the palm branches: immediately the children would snatch their <term>lulavim</term> and eat their <term>etrogim</term>. 
The Hallel and the Rejoicing are eight. How? This teaches that a person is obligated in the Hallel and the rejoicing on the last day of the festival, just like the other days of the festival. The <term>sukkah</term> is seven. How? When he finishes eating, he should not take down his <term>sukkah</term>, but he may take down his utensils from the afternoon onwards for the sake of the honor of the last day of the festival. 
The water libation is seven. How? A gold flask held three <term>log</term> <gloss>a unit of liquid measure</gloss>. He would fill it from the Siloam [spring]. When they reached the Water Gate, they blew the <term>shofar</term>, sounded a <term>teruah</term>, and blew the <term>shofar</term>. He went up to the ramp and turned to his left. There were two silver bowls there. Rabbi Yehuda says: They were of plaster, but they were blackened because of the water and wine, and they were perforated like two nostrils, one wide and one narrow, so that they would both empty at the same time. The western one for water, the eastern for wine. If he poured water into the wine [bowl] or wine into the water, he has fulfilled the requirement. ## On the Righteous and the Sins of the Generation

These words are from my teachers and masters, and I have heard a proper reasoning for what the Rabbi, the author of the *Torat Hayyim*, wrote regarding the matter of the righteous. <note>original: "Torat Hayyim," a prominent 17th-century legal and homiletic work by Rabbi Abraham Hayyim Schor.</note> The righteous are seized and held accountable for the sin of their generation. This occurs because the <term>Attribute of Justice (Middat ha-Din)</term> <note>The aspect of God that demands strict judgment and punishment for sins.</note> desires to destroy the world when the people do not perform the will of the Place. <note>original: "Ha-Makom," a traditional Hebrew name for God implying His omnipresence.</note> 

It is a received tradition that in His mercy, God has compassion for all His works. Therefore, the Holy One, Blessed be He, partnered the <term>Attribute of Mercy (Middat ha-Rahamim)</term> <note>The aspect of God that emphasizes forgiveness and compassion.</note>—which is the predominant force—with the Attribute of Justice. However, the Attribute of Justice continues to prosecute. It requests that the Holy One, Blessed be He, execute judgment in the world. 

The Holy One, Blessed be He, satisfies this demand through one <term>Tzaddik</term> <note>A righteous or saintly person whose spiritual merit protects others.</note> who is considered equal to the entire world. It is written that a righteous person is taken during his lifetime as an atonement. As one sun sets, another sun rises. <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:5, used by the Sages to explain that when one righteous leader dies, another is born to take their place.</note>

Even though this creates a spiritual tension, it is similar to the themes found in the <term>Verses of Praise</term>. <note>original: "Pesukei de-Zimra," a section of the daily morning prayer service.</note> This explains the matter of Haman. When Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow or prostrate himself, Haman was filled with wrath. It seemed beneath him to lay a hand only on Mordecai. Instead, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the entire kingdom of Ahasuerus along with Mordecai. 

A difficulty arises here: Mordecai alone refused to bow, so why did Haman seek to uproot and eradicate all the Jews? The apparent answer is that the generation was already liable for destruction. They had sinned either by bowing to the image of Nebuchadnezzar in the past or by enjoying the forbidden feast of the wicked King Ahasuerus. The wicked Haman acted as a prosecutor in this matter. These matters are from the mouths of my teachers and rabbis, and I have heard a proper explanation. The author of the book <term>Torat Hayyim</term> <gloss>The Torah of Life, a commentary by Rabbi Avraham Chayyim Schorr</gloss> wrote regarding the matter of why the righteous are seized for the sins of the generation. It is because the Attribute of Justice <note>original: middat ha-din</note> seeks to destroy the world when people do not perform the will of the Omnipresent. It is received by tradition that God, in His mercy, has compassion for all His creations. Therefore, the Holy One, Blessed be He, partners the Attribute of Mercy—which is dominant—with the Attribute of Justice. However, the Attribute of Justice prosecutes and demands that the Holy One, Blessed be He, execute judgment in the world. This the Holy One, Blessed be He, performs through one righteous person who is weighed against the entire world. As it is written, a righteous person takes his portion in life <unclear>and so on</unclear>; one righteous person passes away, and the sun rises and the sun sets. 

And even though this causes a prosecution, it is similar to the verses of praise <note>original: pesukei d'zimra</note>. And this is the matter: "Haman saw Mordecai, that he did not kneel or bow to him, and Haman was filled with wrath. But it was contemptible in his eyes to lay hands on Mordecai alone... Haman sought to destroy all the Jews who were in the entire kingdom of Ahasuerus, along with Mordecai." As it is said: it is difficult to understand why, if Mordecai alone refused to bow, Haman sought to uproot and eradicate all the Jews. It seems the answer is that it is known that the generation was liable for destruction because they had bowed to the idol of Nebuchadnezzar, or because they had benefited from the feast of that wicked man, Ahasuerus. Now, the wicked Haman was the prosecutor regarding this, and the Attribute of Justice dictated that they should all die. Therefore, Haman was aroused so that the Holy One, Blessed be He—

<margin>Time</margin>
<margin>Judgments on affairs</margin>

The end of spring, the delay of autumn, summer as the entirety of the hot season, and winter as the entirety of the cold season. Each of the spring and autumn seasons is superior to the other according to the degree of their transition. It seems that spring is the season of balance, as well as fruits, and autumn is the season of leaf changes, as well as their smallness and what arises from them in winter. We say that spring is the moderate temperament, though not as hot as possible, while summer is hot due to the sun and the intensity of its prevailing rays in general upon its members, owing to the step that falls between them, encompassing the place where the sun sets on the earth. It is as if the scorched [region] is isolated from the center of the sun at a time that is equivalent to the simple, or the encompassing, or the setting of the sun. The closest to it is its heat, as the influence is directed toward it from all directions. As for what is in the directions that are weaker, autumn and summer are stronger. By this we mean our cause, meaning the settling of the veins within us. In winter, where it approaches the periphery, for that reason the movement in summer is more intense than the distance from our position and the position of the sun in it. Since it is near, it is necessary that what we name from the west and what is considered from the southern part of spring, by nature, is for the cause. And summer, with the breaking of the ties in it, is the place where rides are taken, because of the period of heat and to endure the day of cold, and its similarity to the fiery nature, and for a cause that is facing medicine and rains. Winter is cold, and the harm from the air in autumn is from what is benefited by it, and what follows it is necessary. As for what approaches balance in the atmosphere, the temperament is moderate in humidity and dryness. How, and the hexagon? It returned from the air, some of it being heat for the important causes. Does it dissolve the incoming cause? The state in cooling is not like the state in preparation, for the healthy towards coldness will be humidity, and the inclination towards humidity will not be universal, and it is slower; it is not the inclination towards heat.

<margin>Time</margin>
<margin>Rulings on affairs</margin>

The end of spring, the delay of autumn and summer, and the entire warm period, as well as winter and the entire cold period, occur. Each of the spring and autumn periods is superior to the other depending on the reaching <note>the state of maturity or peak effect</note>. It seems that spring is the time of balance. This is also true of fruits, while autumn is the time of the changing of leaves, their shrinkage, and what becomes of them in winter. We say spring is the balanced temperament, and it is not as one might assume, which is hot. Summer is hot due to the sun and the presence of direct rays, generally affecting the limbs from the progression that occurs between them, enveloping where the sun falls upon the earth. It is as if the scorched area is separated from the center of the sun at a time that acts as a simple, surrounding, or setting point for the sun. Closer to it is its intense heat <term>samam</term> <gloss>poisonous hot wind/sirocco</gloss>, as the effect is directed toward it from all directions. As for what is in the directions regarding weakness, the autumn of summer is stronger than it. By this, we aim to explain our illness, meaning the settling of the veins within us. In winter, it is close to the periphery; therefore, what is in the summer is more distant from our position than the position of the sun, being close, which necessitates that what we call the west and what is considered from the southern part of spring is natural in its cause. Summer, with the interruption of the winds within it, is the place of stagnation due to the period of heat and the endurance of the cold day, and its resemblance to the fiery nature. This is for the cause of what is directed from medicine and rains. Winter is cold, and the harm from the air in autumn is from what is benefited by it and what follows it. As for what is close to balance in the atmosphere, the temperament is balanced in moisture and dryness. How could it be otherwise? The hexagon <note>likely referring to the geometric influence of celestial movements</note> returned from the air, some of it being among the important causes. Does it dissolve the incoming illness? The situation in cooling is not the same as the situation in preparation, for the healthy are inclined toward coldness in moisture, and the inclination toward moisture is not universal; it is slower than the inclination toward heat.

Regarding the passing of spring, the delay of autumn, and summer being the entire hot season, while winter is the entire cold season: the seasons of spring and autumn are each superior to the other depending on their reach. It seems that spring is the season of moderation, as well as fruits, while autumn is the season of leaf change, their diminution, and what remains of them in winter. We say spring is the moderate <term>mizaj</term> <gloss>temperament/constitution</gloss>, and it is not, as some might think, hot. Summer is hot due to the sun and the presence of intense rays generally covering the limbs from the path that falls between them, encompassing the place where the sun sets on the earth. For it is as if the burned area retreats from the center of the sun at a time that is like a point of simple or ambient light, or the setting of the sun, and closer to it is its pestilence, since the effect is directed toward it from all directions. 

As for what is in the directions regarding weakness, the autumn of summer is stronger than it. By this, we intend our cause, meaning the settling of the veins. In winter, it is close to the circumference, and therefore the heat in summer is more distant from the distance of our position and the position of the sun. Being close, it is necessary that what we name from the west and what is considered from the southern part of spring is natural because of the cause. Summer, with the interruption of the winds within it, is the place of stagnation due to the intensity of heat and the endurance of cold days and its resemblance to the fiery nature. For the cause and the aspect of medicine and rains, winter is cold. The harm from the air in autumn comes from what benefits from it and what follows it. As for that which is close to moderation in the atmosphere, the temperament is moderate in humidity and dryness. How, and the hexagon, it returned from the air, some of it being worthy of significant illnesses. Does it dissolve the coming illness? The situation in cooling is not like the situation in preparation, for healthy people toward coldness tend to have humidity, and the tendency toward humidity is not comprehensive; it is slower than the tendency toward heat.

<margin>Time</margin>
<margin>Judgments on matters</margin>

The passing of spring and the delay of autumn and summer; all of the hot season and winter; all of the cold season. The seasons of spring and autumn are each better than the other in terms of reaching their full extent. It is likely that spring is the time of balance <note>original: "al-i'tidal"</note>, and also of fruits, while autumn is the time of leaves changing and also becoming smaller, and whatever comes of them in winter. We say that spring is the balanced temperament <note>original: "al-mizaj al-mu'tadil"</note> and is not merely what is possible in being hot. Summer is hot in the sun and from the perspective of the height and force of the covering rays generally hitting its parts from the line that falls between them, surrounding where the sun strikes the earth. It is as if the scorched area is isolated from the center of the sun. Time is in the position of the simple, the surrounding, or the setting of the sun, and closer to its zenith, as the influence is directed to it from all sides. As for what is in the regions of the weaker end of summer and its autumn, it is stronger than it. We seek through it our cause, meaning the habitation of the veins. In winter, it is where it approaches the surrounding. For that reason, growth in summer is more cautious than the distance from our station to the sun's station when it is near. It is necessary that what we perceive from the west and what is considered from the southern part of spring is natural to the cause. Summer, with the cutting of the connections in it, is the place for accumulations from the period of heat, to bear the day of cold and its resemblance to the fiery nature, and for a cause and guidance from medicine and rains. Winter is cold, and from the harm of the air in autumn is whoever benefited from it. What is necessary is what follows it. As for what is near to balance in the atmosphere, the temperament is balanced in moisture and dryness. How, then, when the sextile <note>likely an astrological reference to the 60-degree angle</note> returns some of the air with significant illnesses? Does it dissolve the coming illness? The state in cooling is not like the state in preparation; the healthy towards coldness have moisture, and the tendency toward moisture is not comprehensive and is slower; the tendency toward heat is not the same.

Reclining therein on thrones, excellent is the reward and good is the resting place. And present to them an example of two men, for one of whom We had made two gardens of grapevines and surrounded them with palm trees and placed between them crops. Each of the two gardens brought forth its fruit and did not fail in it at all, and We caused to gush forth within them a river. And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while he was conversing with him, I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in number of men. And he entered his garden while he was unjust to himself. He said, I do not think that this will perish ever. And I do not think the Hour will occur. And even if I should be brought back to my Lord, I will surely find

<column-break/>

better than it as a return. His companion said to him while he was conversing with him, Have you disbelieved in He who created you from dust and then from a drop <note>a sperm-drop</note>, then fashioned you a man? But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate with my Lord anyone. And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, What Allah willed, there is no power except by Allah? If you see me less than you in wealth and children, then it may be that my Lord will give me better than your garden and will send upon it a calamity from the sky, and it will become a slippery ground, or its water will become sunken <note>deep in the earth</note>, so you would never be able to seek it. And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his hands over <note>in regret</note> for what he had spent.

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of the First Cause, moving from the problem of evil to the metaphysical definitions of existence and duration. It specifically addresses debates regarding how things persist over time.</meta>

...toward correctness. Perhaps this account is closer to the truth upon first consideration and a superficial look, provided one does not falter in nonsense or get lost in myths. In such a case, these two paths would be very far from the truth. 

As for <margin>Persistence</margin> the discourse regarding persistence <term>al-baqāʾ</term> <note>original: "al-baqāʾ"; the quality of remaining in existence over time, often debated as to whether it is a distinct attribute or just existence itself.</note> and the persistent, it is a matter that has captivated a group of fools. They have neither understood nor perceived the truth. Persistence is nothing more than the existent <term>al-mawjūd</term> being characterized by existence <term>al-wujūd</term> for a certain duration. Existence is viewed without regard to duration. Persistence is existence considered within the meaning of duration. 

Therefore, existence is a more general concept than persistence. The difference between existence and persistence is only a matter of generality and specificity. It is surprising that the person who holds this view [the opposing view] admits that existence and the existent are a single meaning in external reality, even if they are distinct in the mind. The same rule must apply to persistence. 

As for the dialectical discourse that forces them to commit basic absurdities, it is as follows. They ask: Is there anything here described by persistence? If they answer "no," it is said to them: then there is nothing persistent here. What then is it that brings beings into existence and keeps them in existence, according to your claim, <margin>In moments</margin> through the succession of continuous acts of creation? 

This is despite the fact that a logical proof <term>al-burhān</term> has established the invalidity of successive moments <note>The author is likely refuting the "atomist" view held by some theologians who believed time consists of discrete, disconnected "now" moments rather than a continuous flow.</note>. However, we shall be lenient with you. If they answer that this source of succession is not persistent, they fall into the most impossible and ugliest of absurdities. I suspect they wish to avoid such a conclusion.

<summary>The author clarifies the relationship between existence and persistence, arguing that persistence is simply existence viewed through the lens of duration. He uses this logic to critique theological opponents who claim that the world is recreated in discrete, successive moments.</summary>
<keywords>existence, persistence, duration, metaphysics, logic, Ibn Sina, instants, causality, duration</keywords>

...towards the truth, for perhaps the report is closer to the truth in the initial opinion and the superficial view, without stuttering in delirium or sinking into its <note>the opponent's</note> myths. For if one does so, one becomes very far from the truth. As for the <margin>Persistence</margin> discourse current regarding the "persistent" <term>al-baqi</term> <gloss>the persistent/remaining</gloss> and "persistence" <term>al-baqa'</term> <gloss>persistence/permanence</gloss>, it is a matter with which a group of foolish people have become infatuated, as they have not grasped or discerned the truth. Persistence is nothing but the attribute of a being <term>al-mawjud</term> <gloss>the existing thing</gloss> having existence for a certain duration. Thus, existence does not concern itself with duration, whereas persistence is existence within the meaning of duration. Existence is a broader concept than persistence, so the difference between existence and persistence is only one of specificity and generality. Furthermore, it is astonishing that the proponent of this view admits that existence <term>al-wujud</term> <gloss>existence</gloss> and the existing thing are one and the same meaning in reality, even if they differ in the mind.
