Good and evil are not equal. Repel evil with that which is better, and then the one between whom and you there is enmity will be as a close friend. And none is granted this except those who are patient, and none is granted this except one having a great portion of good. And if an evil suggestion from Satan comes to you, then seek refuge in God. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing. And of His signs are the night and the day and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to God, who created them, if you worship Him. But if they are arrogant, those who are with your Lord exalt Him by night and day, and they are not weary. And of His signs is that you see the earth humbled, but when We send down upon it water, it quivers and grows. Indeed, He who has revived it is the Giver of Life to the dead. Indeed, He is over all things competent. Indeed, those who distort Our signs are not hidden from Us. So, is he who is cast into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection? Do as you will; indeed, He is Seeing of what you do. Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Message when it comes to them—and indeed, it is a mighty Book. Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it. It is a revelation from a Wise, Praiseworthy One. Nothing is said to you except what was already said to the messengers before you. Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness and full of painful punishment. And if We had made it a non-Arabic Quran, they would have said, "Why were its verses not clarified? Is it foreign and Arabic?" Say, "It is, for those who believe, a guidance and cure." And those who do not believe—in their ears is deafness, and it is upon them blindness. Those are being called from a distant place. And We gave Moses the Scripture, but disagreement occurred over it. And if not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them. And indeed, they are, concerning it, in disquieting doubt. Whoever does righteousness, it is for his soul, and whoever does evil, it is against it. And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants.

To Him is returned the knowledge of the Hour. And no fruit emerges from its spathes, and no female carries or gives birth except with His knowledge. And on the Day He will call to them, "Where are My partners?" They will say, "We announce to You that there is among us no witness." And lost from them will be those they were invoking before, and they will realize that they have no place of escape. Man does not tire of praying for good, but if evil touches him, he is despairing and hopeless. And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, "This is mine, and I do not think the Hour will be established. And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed, I will have with Him the best." But We will surely inform those who disbelieved about what they did, and We will surely make them taste a harsh punishment. And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself, and when evil touches him, then he is full of extensive supplication. Say, "Have you considered: if it is from God and you disbelieved in it, who is more astray than one who is in distant opposition?" We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. But is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness? Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord. Unquestionably, He is, of all things, encompassing.

He arranged the markets to surround the Great Mosque on the eastern side of the Nile. He established a guard post and an overseer for every tribe. He also built the Giza fortress on the western side of the Nile, making it a military outpost for the Muslims and settling a group of people there. He wrote to <margin>119</margin> Umar ibn al-Khattab regarding this, but Umar wrote back to him: Do not put water between me and the Muslims. Amr conquered the provinces of Egypt through peace treaties, except for Alexandria. He remained there fighting <margin>5</margin> its people for three years before conquering it in the year 23 <note>643–644 CE</note>, because no other city in the land equaled it in fortification, size, and abundance of resources.

The provinces of Egypt are named after their cities, for every province has a city distinguished by a particular characteristic. Among the cities of Upper Egypt and its provinces is the city of Memphis <note>original: "Manf"</note>, which is a standing <margin>a)</margin> ruin <note>The editor notes a reader likely corrected this to "ancient city"</note>. The people of Egypt say it is the city where Pharaoh used to reside. There is also the city of Busir Kuridis <margin>10 b)</margin> and the city of Dalas, to which the <term>Dalasite</term> bridles are attributed. Then there is the city of al-Fayyum; in former times, people used to say Egypt and al-Fayyum because of the majesty of al-Fayyum and its extensive cultivation. It produces the renowned wheat and is where <term>khaysh</term> <gloss>coarse linen or burlap</gloss> <margin>c)</margin> is manufactured.

There is the city of al-Qays, where the <term>Qaysite</term> garments and high-quality wool cloaks are made. There is the city of al-Bahnasa, where the <margin>f. 65 r.</margin> <term>Bahnasite</term> veils are made. Then there is the city of Ahnas, where cloaks are made and where the <margin>15</margin> <term>labakh</term> <gloss>lebbek</gloss> trees <margin>d)</margin> grow. There is the city of Taha, which produces renowned wheat and the jugs that the people of Egypt call <term>bawāqīl</term>. There is Antinoöpolis <note>original: "Ansanā"</note>, an ancient city said to be the home of Pharaoh’s magicians, and it is claimed that remnants of magic still exist there. It is located on the eastern side of the Nile. There is also the city of al-Ashmunayn, known for the excellence of its horses, beasts of burden, and mules; it is one of the great cities of Egypt. Finally, there is the city of Asyut, one of the major cities of Upper Egypt, <margin>20</margin> where <term>qirmiz</term> <gloss>crimson</gloss> carpets are made that resemble Armenian work. endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, an knower of the worlds, an incomparable trainer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. He makes known this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans, having realized it through his own supernormal knowledge. He teaches the Dhamma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right phrasing, and he reveals the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. A householder or a householder's son, or one born in some other clan, hears that Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.

Possessing that gain of faith, he considers this: "The household life is narrow, a path of dust; the homeless life is like the open air. It is not easy for one who lives in a house to lead the holy life that is entirely complete, entirely pure, and polished like a conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?" So, after some time, he abandons his wealth, small or large, abandons his circle of relatives, small or large, shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness.

So, having gone forth, he lives endowed with the training and the livelihood of the monks, having abandoned the taking of life, he refrains from taking life. He dwells with the rod laid down, the weapon laid down, conscientious, merciful, and kind to all living beings. Having abandoned the taking of what is not given, he refrains from taking what is not given. He is an acceptor of what is given, a waiter for what is given, and he dwells with a pure and honest self. Having abandoned unchastity, he is a holy celibate, refraining from the common sexual practice. Having abandoned false speech, he refrains from false speech. He is a speaker of truth, a dweller in truth, steadfast, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world. Having abandoned malicious speech, he refrains from malicious speech. He does not tell what he has heard here to those over there in order to cause division among them, nor does he tell what he has heard there to those over here in order to cause division among them. Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are united, rejoicing in harmony, delighted in harmony, fond of harmony, a speaker of words that create harmony. Having abandoned harsh speech, he refrains from harsh speech. He speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, polite, desired by many, and liked by many. Having abandoned idle chatter...

### FOUR INDIVIDUALS.

Endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, knower of the worlds, the unsurpassed trainer of tamable persons, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One: he, having realized it by his own direct knowledge, makes known this world with its gods, Maras, and Brahmas, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans. He teaches the doctrine that is beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end, in both meaning and phrasing, and he reveals a spiritual life that is completely perfect and pure. A householder, or the son of a householder, or someone reborn in another family, hears that doctrine. Having heard that doctrine, he gains faith in the Tathagata.

Endowed with that acquisition of faith, he reflects thus: "The household life is cramped, a path of dust, while the life of renunciation is like the open air. It is not easy for one who lives in a house to lead the holy life as perfectly and purely as a polished shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?" So, after a time, he abandons a small or large store of wealth, and he abandons a small or large circle of relatives, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness.

Having thus gone forth, he lives endowed with the training and way of life of the monks. Abandoning the taking of life, he abstains from taking life, has laid down the club and the sword, is scrupulous, merciful, and dwells compassionate toward all living beings. Abandoning the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given, takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and lives by a self that is honest and pure. Abandoning unchastity, he practices the holy life, living apart and abstaining from the sexual act, the village practice. Abandoning false speech, he abstains from false speech, is a speaker of truth, reliable, trustworthy, and does not deceive the world. Abandoning divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech. Having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere in order to cause division; having heard something elsewhere, he does not repeat it here in order to cause division. Thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a supporter of those who are united; he rejoices in harmony, delights in harmony, loves harmony, and speaks words that promote harmony. Abandoning harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovely, going to the heart, courteous, desired by many, and dear to many. Abandoning idle chatter <note>The text breaks off here mid-sentence, but "samphappalāpaṃ" means "idle chatter."</note>

The fourth jhānas of the knowledge of reading others' minds, knowledge of past lives, and knowledge of the future, however, are path-objects when they arise knowing the path-consciousness of noble ones. Because they are not co-nascent with the path, they are not path-conditioned; and because they do not arise holding the path in high regard, they are not path-dominated. Why do they not hold the path in high regard? Because of their own exalted state. Just as the whole world holds a king in high regard, but his own parents do not—for they do not rise from their seats upon seeing the king, nor do they perform acts of homage, but treat him according to the customs of when he was young—so, too, these do not hold the path in high regard because of their own exalted state.

Even the rootless functional mind-consciousness-element, at the time noble ones reflect on the path, is a path-object because it is the forerunner to that reflection. But because it is not co-nascent with the path, it is not path-conditioned, and because it does not arise holding <note>the path</note> in high regard, it is not path-dominated. Why does it not hold it in high regard? Because of its own lack of roots, its inferiority, and its dullness. Just as the whole world holds a king in high regard, but his inner circle, such as the hunchbacked, dwarfs, and servants, do not hold him in high regard—thinking themselves like learned people due to their own ignorance—so, too, this consciousness does not hold the path in high regard because of its lack of roots, its inferiority, and its dullness. Wholesome <note>consciousnesses</note> dissociated from knowledge and the like do not attain the status of path-objects due to the nature of <note>their</note> knowledge and because their object is a worldly state; they should be understood as having objects that are "not to be spoken of."

If at the time when one of the <term>chanda</term> <gloss>desire</gloss> or <term>citta</term> <gloss>consciousness</gloss> factors is chief, it is not to be said that there is a <term>maggādhipati</term>. However, the <term>cetopariyañāṇa</term> <gloss>knowledge of the minds of others</gloss>, <term>pubbenivāsañāṇa</term> <gloss>knowledge of past lives</gloss>, and <term>anāgata-saññāṇa</term> <gloss>knowledge of the future</gloss>—these four, when noble ones know the path-consciousness, become objects of the path. Because they do not co-arise with the path, they are not caused by the path; and because they do not function by making the path supreme, they are not dominated by the path. And why do they not make the path supreme? Because of their own <term>mahaggatattā</term> <gloss>state of being sublime/great</gloss>. Just as the whole world honors a king, but his mother and father do not—for they do not rise from their seats upon seeing the king, nor do they perform acts of homage like the <term>añjali</term> <gloss>salutation with joined palms</gloss>, but rather they speak to him just as they spoke in his childhood—so too, these states do not make the path supreme because of their own sublimity.

The <term>kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu</term> <gloss>functional mind-consciousness element with roots</gloss> of noble ones is also an object of the path at the time of reviewing the path, because it precedes the review. However, because it does not co-arise with the path, it is not caused by the path, and because it does not function by making [the path] supreme, it is not dominated by the path. And why does it not make it supreme? Because of its being <term>ahetuka</term> <gloss>rootless</gloss>, its inferiority, and its dullness. Just as the whole world honors a king, but his inner retinue—such as hunchbacks, dwarfs, and servants—do not honor him because of their own ignorance, just as if they were people of wisdom, in the same way, this consciousness does not make the path supreme because of its own rootlessness, inferiority, and dullness. It should be understood that wholesome states dissociated from knowledge and the like do not attain the state of being an object of the path, etc., because they lack the nature of knowledge and because their object is the sphere of mundane phenomena; they are simply states that are not to be spoken of [as having the path as an object].

Or, having made one of them the leader, at the time of cultivating the path, it may be a path-predominance <term>maggādhipati</term> <gloss>dominance consisting of the path</gloss> by way of a co-arisen condition. Regarding the time when one of the desires or consciousnesses becomes the leader of the path-predominance, it should not be said that they are path-predominances. In the twelve types of fourth <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> of the form-sphere, the nine <term>jhānas</term> starting from the fourth <term>jhāna</term> which serves as a basis for all others, are neither based on the path, nor caused by the path, nor governed by the path.

However, the four—knowledge of the minds of others, knowledge of previous lives, knowledge of the future, and the fourth <term>jhāna</term>—when they occur at the time a noble person knows their own path-consciousness, have the path as their object. Because they are not co-arisen with the path, they are not caused by the path; and because they do not occur by treating the path as a superior object, they are not governed by the path. Why do these not treat the path as a superior object? Because of their own exalted <term>mahaggata</term> <gloss>great/exalted</gloss> nature. Just as the whole world honors a king, but his parents do not—for they do not rise from their seats upon seeing the king, nor do they perform salutations or similar acts, but treat him according to the way they spoke of him when he was a child—in the same way, these states, due to their own exalted nature, do not treat the path as a superior object.

The functional <term>kiriya</term> <gloss>inoperative/functional</gloss> mind-element without roots <term>ahetuka</term> <gloss>rootless</gloss>, even at the time a noble person reviews the path, serves as a reviewer and has the path as its object. Yet, because it is not co-arisen with the path, it is not caused by the path, and because it does not occur by treating it as a superior object, it is not governed by the path. Why does it not treat it as a superior object? Because of its rootless nature, its inferiority, and its dullness. Just as the whole world honors a king, but his inner servants—the hunchbacks, dwarves, and errand-boys—do not treat him with honor, like wise people would, because of their own ignorance, so too this consciousness, due to its rootless nature, its inferiority, and its dullness, does not treat the path as a superior object. It should be understood that wholesome states disconnected from knowledge and the like do not attain the status of having the path as an object, and so on, both because they lack knowledge and because they have mundane states as their objects; they should be known as having objects that are not to be spoken of in this way.

# Verses of the Elder Nuns. 59.

These three were the younger sisters of the General of the Dhamma <note>original: "dhammasenāpatissa"; referring to Sariputta, the Buddha's chief disciple</note>. The names of their three sons were also the same, which is why they are referred to in the verses of the Elder Nuns as Cala, Upacala, and Sisupacala. When these three sisters heard that the General of the Dhamma had gone forth into the homeless life, they were filled with inspiration and intense desire, thinking, "Surely that Teaching and Discipline is not inferior, nor is that going forth inferior, wherein our noble brother has gone forth." Leaving behind their weeping relatives and attendants with tearful faces, they went forth. Having gone forth, they exerted themselves and strove, and before long they attained <term>arahantship</term> <gloss>the state of an enlightened being</gloss>. Having attained <term>arahantship</term>, they dwelt in the happiness of <term>nibbana</term> <gloss>liberation</gloss> and the happiness of the fruit of the path. One day, the nun Cala, having returned from her alms round after her meal, entered the Blind Men's Grove <note>original: "Andhavanam"</note> and sat down for her day-rest. Then Mara <note>the tempter or personification of death and desire</note> approached her and tried to seduce her with sensual pleasures, as is recounted in the scripture.

Then the nun Cala, having dressed in the morning and taking her bowl and robe, entered Savatthi for alms. Having walked for alms in Savatthi and returned from her alms round after her meal, she approached the Joyful Grove <note>original: "Nandavanam"</note> for her day-rest. Having approached and entered deep into the Blind Men's Grove, she sat at the foot of a certain tree for her day-rest. Then Mara the Evil One approached the nun Cala and said this to her: Mara, wishing to detach her from the holy life while she sat for her day-rest in the Blind Men's Grove, asked, "On whose account have you shaved your head?" and so forth. Then, by proclaiming the virtues of the Teacher and the leading-out nature of the Dhamma, and by explaining that she had completed her task, she declared her transcendence of Mara's domain. Hearing this, Mara, sad and dejected, vanished right there. Then, she spoke the verses uttered by herself and Mara as an inspired utterance:

The nun, having established mindfulness and developed her faculties,
penetrated the state of peace, the happiness of the stilling of formations. 182.
"On whose account have you shaved your head? You look like a female ascetic..."

These three were the younger sisters of the General of the Dharma <note>original: "dhammasenāpati"; a title for Sāriputta.</note>. These three sisters, having heard that the General of the Dharma had gone forth, thought, "That teaching and discipline is certainly not base, nor is that going forth base, since our elder brother has gone forth." Inspired and filled with intense desire, they abandoned their weeping relatives with tear-stained faces and went forth. Having gone forth, striving and exerting themselves, they attained <term>arahatta</term> <gloss>the state of the worthy one; enlightenment</gloss> before long. Having attained <term>arahatta</term>, they lived in the bliss of <term>nibbāna</term> <gloss>extinction of the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion</gloss> and the bliss of the fruits <note>of the path</note>. One day, after her meal and upon returning from her alms round, the nun Cālā entered the Andhavana forest and sat down for her day-resting. Then Māra approached her and tempted her with sensual desires, in reference to which it is stated in the discourse.

Then the nun Cālā, having dressed in the morning and taking her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned after her meal, she went to the Nandavana grove for her day-resting. Inspired and filled with keen desire, they abandoned their relatives and attendants who were weeping with tearful faces and went forth. Having gone forth, they strove and exerted themselves and before long attained <term>arahattaship</term> <gloss>the state of a perfected one</gloss>. Having attained <term>arahattaship</term>, they lived experiencing the bliss of <term>nibbāna</term> <gloss>the state of extinction of suffering</gloss> and the bliss of the fruits <note>of the path</note>. One day, after her meal, the nun Cālā returned from the alms round, entered the Andha Forest, and sat down to spend the day. Then Māra approached her and tempted her with sensual pleasures, regarding which it is said in the sutta:

Then the nun Cālā, having dressed in the morning, took her bowl and robe and entered Sāvatthi for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthi and returned from the alms round after her meal, she approached the Nanda Grove to spend the day. Having approached, she plunged into the Andha Forest and sat at the root of a tree to spend the day. Then Māra the Evil One approached the nun Cālā, and having approached, he said this to the nun Cālā: sitting in the Andha Forest to spend the day, Māra approached her, wishing to cut her off from her life of celibacy, and asked: "Whom are you aiming at in being shaven, like a renunciant?" And so on. Then, having proclaimed the virtues of the Teacher and the liberating nature of the Dharma, she declared her own transcendence of his domain by demonstrating that her tasks were done. Hearing that, Māra, miserable and dejected, vanished right there. Then she spoke the verses that were spoken by herself and Māra in the form of an inspired utterance:

Has penetrated the peaceful state, the happiness of the calming of formations. 182.
Whom are you aiming at in being shaven, appearing like a renunciant?

The three women were the younger sisters of the <term>Dhammasenāpati</term> <gloss>General of the Dhamma, an epithet for Sāriputta</gloss>. Their three sons also shared the same names. It is in reference to these three sisters that the names Cālā, Upacālā, and Sisūpacālā appear in the <term>Therīgāthā</term> <gloss>Verses of the Elder Nuns</gloss>. 

When these three sisters heard that the General of the Dhamma had gone forth into the homeless life, they were filled with energy and intense desire. They thought: Surely that teaching and discipline are not inferior, and that renunciation is not inferior, since our noble brother has gone forth there. They left behind their relatives and attendants who were weeping with tearful faces and they also went forth. Having gone forth, they exerted themselves and strove until they soon attained <term>arahatta</term> <gloss>the state of enlightenment</gloss>. After attaining enlightenment, they lived experiencing the bliss of <term>Nibbāna</term> <gloss>the final liberation</gloss> and the bliss of the fruition of the path. 

One day, after the midday meal, the nun Cālā returned from her alms round and entered the Andhavana forest. She sat down for her afternoon rest. Then Māra <note>the personification of death, desire, and delusion</note> approached her and tried to entice her with sensual pleasures, as is described in the discourse.

Then the nun Cālā, having dressed in the morning and taking her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthi for alms. After walking for alms in Sāvatthi and returning from her alms round after the meal, she went toward the Nandavana forest for her afternoon rest. Having arrived, she plunged into the Andhavana forest and sat at the foot of a certain tree for her afternoon rest. 

Then Māra the Evil One approached the nun Cālā. Having approached her, he said this: Māra, wanting to divert her from the holy life as she sat for her afternoon rest in the Andhavana forest, asked: On whose account have you shaved your head? and so on. Then, she declared the qualities of the Teacher and the liberating nature of the Dhamma. By explaining that she had completed her task, she announced that she had transcended his domain. Hearing this, Māra, sad and dejected, vanished right there. Then, she recited the verses spoken by herself and Māra as an inspired utterance:

Establishing her mindfulness, the nun with developed faculties
Penetrated the state of peace, the bliss of the stilling of formations. (Verse 182)
On whose account have you shaved your head? You look like a female ascetic...

Then the Blessed One, together with many monks, went to the Black Rock on Mount Isigili. The Blessed One saw from afar the venerable Godhika lying with his body turned aside. At that time, a smoky, dark cloud was moving toward the east, toward the west, toward the north, toward the south, toward the zenith, toward the nadir, and toward the intermediate directions.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Do you see, monks, that smoky, dark cloud moving toward the east, toward the west, toward the north, toward the south, toward the zenith, toward the nadir, and toward the intermediate directions?" "Yes, Lord." "That, monks, is Mara the Evil One, searching for the consciousness of the clansman Godhika, wondering, 'Where is the consciousness of the clansman Godhika established?' But, monks, with consciousness unestablished, the clansman Godhika is fully quenched."

Then Mara the Evil One, assuming the appearance of a youth, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he addressed the Blessed One with a verse:

"Upward, downward, and across, in all directions I have searched,
I cannot find Godhika; where has he gone?"

"The steadfast one, endowed with vision, meditative and always devoted to <term>jhana</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>,
Day and night he applies himself, not desiring life,
Having conquered the army of Death, without returning to rebirth,
Having pulled out craving by the root, he is fully quenched."

Then the Blessed One, accompanied by many monks, went to the Black Rock <note>original: "Kālasilā"</note> on the Isigili slope. There, the Blessed One saw the venerable Godhika lying on his side on the path, his consciousness withdrawn. At that time, a smoky, darkened cloud was moving, going toward the eastern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, upward, downward, and toward the intermediate directions.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Do you see, monks, that smoky, darkened cloud moving toward the eastern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, upward, downward, and toward the intermediate directions?"

"Yes, Blessed One."

"That, monks, is Mara the Wicked, searching for the consciousness of the clansman Godhika, wondering, 'Where has the consciousness of the clansman Godhika been established?' But, monks, the clansman Godhika has attained <term>parinibbāna</term> <gloss>final extinction/liberation</gloss> with an unestablished consciousness."

Then Mara the Wicked, assuming the appearance of a young man, approached the Blessed One and addressed him with a verse:

"Upward, downward, and across, in all directions,
I have searched, yet I do not find where that Godhika has gone."

[The Blessed One replied:]

"The wise one, endowed with right view, devoted to <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>, always delighting in <term>jhāna</term>, 
Applying himself day and night, disregarding life,
Having conquered the army of <term>Maccu</term> <gloss>Death/Mara</gloss>, he does not return to renewed existence."

The Blessed One saw the Venerable <term>Godhika</term> <gloss>a monk who attained liberation at the moment of death</gloss> from afar, lying on his bed with his shoulder turned over. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, do you see that dark cloud of smoke and vapor moving toward the east, the west, the north, the south, upward, downward, and toward the intermediate quarters?”

“Yes, venerable sir.”

He is searching for the <term>vinnana</term> <gloss>consciousness</gloss> of the clansman Godhika, wondering: 'Where has the consciousness of the clansman Godhika become established?' "The agreement of those three was called the partridge's holy life. Indeed, monks, they were animals who lived respectful of one another. The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma talk and having become fully enlightened, spoke this verse:

In this context, "vaddha" <note>elder</note> refers to three kinds: elder by birth, elder by age, and elder by virtue. Among them, one endowed with birth is called elder by birth; one established in age is called elder by age; one endowed with virtue is called elder by virtue. Among them, the one endowed with virtue and elder by age is intended here by "elder." "Apacāyanti" means they honor him with the act of paying respect to the senior. "Dhammassa kovidā" means they are skilled in the teaching of paying respect to the senior. "Diṭṭhe va dhamme" means in this very existence. "Pasaṃsā" means they are worthy of praise. "Samparāye ca suggatī" means for them there is a good destination even in the next life, which is to be attained after leaving this world. This is the gist: Monks, whether they be warriors, brahmins, merchants, workers, householders, those gone forth, or animals, whoever is skilled in the act of paying respect to the senior and pays respect to those elders by age endowed with virtue, they receive praise and commendation as practitioners of respect for the senior in this existence, and upon the breaking up of the body, they are reborn in heaven.

Thus, the Teacher, having spoken of the virtue of paying respect to the senior, connected the context and identified the Jataka: "At that time, the elephant was Moggallāna, the monkey was Sāriputta, but I was the wise partridge." The Tittira Jataka.

<meta>Continuity: Continued description of the Coir Palm growth and physical characteristics.</meta>

It does not wither in any season. The trunk is straight and has no branches. Near the leaves, it is wrapped in bark. Every time it grows a layer, it forms a section. The trunk is red-black, full of veins and fibers. It is suitable for making bell clappers, and can also be turned on a lathe into utensils. Its bark has fibrous threads interlaced like weaving. If stripped and unraveled into threads, it can be woven into clothing, hats, mats, and chairs. This is of great benefit to the era; it must be stripped two or three times a year, otherwise the tree will die or stop growing. In the third month, several yellow buds emerge from the stem at the top of the tree. Inside the buds are fine seeds arranged in rows, which is the embryo of the flower. Its shape is like a fish belly, so the pregnant seeds are called "coir fish" or "coir shoots." As they grow and emerge from the buds, they become flower spikes, yellow and white. The fruit grows in clusters as large as beans; they are green when raw and black when ripe, being very firm and solid. # Turmeric
<gloss>From the "Tang Materia Medica" (Tang Ben Cao)</gloss>

<insert>Names</insert> *Shu* <gloss>pronounced "shù"</gloss>, Treasure Tripod Incense <gloss>From the "Compendium" (Gangmu)</gloss>.

<insert>Explanations</insert> <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> The roots and leaves of Turmeric look exactly like Wild Turmeric (*Yujin*). In spring, its flowers emerge from the roots alongside the sprouts. In summer, the flowers fade without producing seeds. The roots come in three colors: yellow, green, and white. The processing method is the same as for Wild Turmeric. People of the Western Rong <note>historical term for ethnic groups in Western China</note> call it *Shu*. Its taste is slightly pungent and mostly bitter, also similar to Wild Turmeric; only the timing of the flowers differs. <gloss>Chen Zangqi says:</gloss> True Turmeric is actually old Ginger that has been planted for over three years. It produces flowers at the base of the root, looking much like Ginger-lily. The root sections are hard, and the flavor is pungent and spicy. It can be found wherever ginger is grown, but it is rare. Some comes from the Western regions, looking like Wild Turmeric. What Su Gong described is actually Zedoary <term>Zedoary: Curcuma zedoaria, a related but different root</term> rather than Turmeric. He claimed Turmeric is *Shu* and Wild Turmeric is "Foreign *Shu*." If that were true, these three things would be indistinguishable and all called *Shu*, and their effects would be the same. However, Wild Turmeric is bitter and cold, red in color, and primarily treats "horse heat" diseases. Turmeric is pungent and warm, yellow in color. Zedoary is bitter and green. These three are distinct and used differently. <gloss>Li Tianming says:</gloss> That which grows in Hainan is Zedoary; that which grows south of the Yangtze is Turmeric. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Turmeric is now found in many regions like Jiangnan, Guangdong, and Sichuan. The leaves are green, one to two feet long and three to four inches wide, with diagonal veins like small red banana leaves. The flowers are reddish-white and wither by mid-autumn. It sprouts in late spring, flowering first, then leafing. It does not fruit. The roots are yellow, shaped like ginger but rounder and segmented. Harvested in the eighth month, sliced and dried. People in Sichuan use it to treat abdominal "qi" <term>qi: vital energy or physiological function</term> and postpartum "ruined blood" <note>original: "ruined blood" (敗血 - baixue), referring to lochia or stagnant blood after childbirth</note> attacking the heart; it is very effective. The southern tribes eat it raw to ward off evil and pestilence. Note that Wild Turmeric, Turmeric, and Zedoary are so similar that Su Gong could not tell them apart. Chen Zangqi distinguished them by color and taste. Recently, merchants often sell old Ginger as Turmeric to deceive people, claiming it is superior for treating "qi" issues. There is also "Lian-ginger," which is related but a different species. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Nowadays, the flat ones shaped like dried ginger are called "Sliver Turmeric" (Pianzi Jianghuang), and the round ones shaped like a cicada's belly are "Cicada-Belly Wild Turmeric." Both can be soaked to dye water, but while they look like Wild Turmeric, they are not as yellow.

Root <insert>Properties</insert> Pungent and bitter, greatly cold, non-toxic. <gloss>Chen Zangqi says: It is slightly pungent and mostly bitter. It is warm, not cold. The claim of "greatly cold" is an error.</gloss>

<insert>Indications</insert> For accumulations in the heart and abdomen, "clash with the uncanny" <note>original: "zhuwu" (疰忤), a term for sudden illness attributed to malevolent spirits or environmental factors</note>, descending "qi," and breaking stagnant blood. It clears wind-heat and dissolves swellings. Its power is more intense than Wild Turmeric. <gloss>From "Tang Materia Medica"</gloss>. For abdominal masses, blood clots, and regulating menstruation. It treats bruises, stops sudden wind pain, and helps with "cold qi" digestion. <gloss>From "Daming Materia Medica"</gloss>. Treats strikes from evil, abdominal bloating, and postpartum blood attacking the heart. <gloss>Su Song</gloss>. Treats "wind-dampness" (bi) syndrome and arm pain. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss> says: Turmeric, Wild Turmeric, and Zedoary are similar in shape and function, but Turmeric enters the Liver meridian to treat the "blood within the qi." The ancient "Five-Bi Decoction" uses Sliver Turmeric to treat arm pain caused by wind, cold, and dampness. This shows its ability to regulate the "qi within the blood."

# Turmeric (Jianghuang)
<gloss>Tang Materia Medica</gloss>

<insert>Explanation of Name:</insert> <term>Shu</term> <gloss>pronounced "shu"</gloss>, <term>Baodingxiang</term> <gloss>Incense of the Precious Tripod (Compendium)</gloss>.

<insert>Collected Explanations:</insert> <gloss>Gong says:</gloss> The roots and leaves of Turmeric are both like those of <term>Curcuma aromatica</term> (Yujin). Its flowers grow in the spring from the roots, appearing alongside the sprouts. By summer, the flowers rot and do not produce seeds. The roots have yellow, green, and white varieties. The method of preparation is the same as for Yujin. The people of the Western Barbarians call it <term>Shu</term>. Its flavor is pungent with a little bitterness, also like Yujin, but the flowers are different. <gloss>Cangqi says:</gloss> Genuine Turmeric is the old ginger root that has been growing for three years or more, which can produce flowers. The flowers are at the base of the root, just like the ginger lotus. The root joints are hard and the flavor is pungent and spicy. It is found where ginger is planted. It is ultimately hard to obtain. There are also those coming from the Western Barbarians. They are similar to Yujin. What Wu Gong describes is the drug <term>Shu</term> and not Turmeric. He also says Turmeric is <term>Shu</term>, and Yujin is Foreign <term>Shu</term>. Thus, these three things are not different. If they are collectively called <term>Shu</term>, their effects and forms should not be different. Yet now, Yujin is bitter and cold, red in color, and treats horse heat-disease. Turmeric is pungent and warm, yellow in color. <term>Shu</term> is bitter and green. These three things are different, and their uses are distinct. <gloss>Tianming says:</gloss> Those grown in Hainan are <term>Curcuma zedoaria</term> (Pengezhusu), and those grown in Jiangnan are Turmeric. <gloss>Song says:</gloss> Turmeric is now common in Jiang, Guang, and Shu (Sichuan). The leaves are green and long, one to two feet, three to four inches wide, with diagonal veins like red banana leaves but smaller. The flowers are red and white, gradually withering by mid-autumn. They sprout in late spring. The flowers appear first, then the leaves. They do not bear seeds. The roots are curved, yellow, and like raw ginger but round with joints. Harvest the roots in the eighth month, slice them, and dry them in the sun. People of Shu use it to treat abdominal gas and postpartum putrid blood attacking the heart, which is very effective. The barbarians eat it raw, saying it can dispel evil and ward off bad influences. Note: Yujin, Turmeric, and <term>Shu</term> medicine are similar in these three things. Gong could not distinguish them and thought they were one thing. Chen Cangqi distinguished the three things by color and flavor and also said Turmeric is the root of three-year-old ginger. In recent years, there is much juice; when planting ginger, Turmeric often grows. It is truly just old ginger. Market merchants buy it and falsely claim it treats gas. It is a major prescription and often used. There is also "Leong" ginger, which is of the same class but a different thing. Shizhen says: Recently, those shaped like dried ginger are called "slice Turmeric," and those shaped like cicada abdomens are "cicada belly Yujin." Both can be soaked in water to dye colors, but though the shape is like Yujin, the color is not yellow.

Root <insert>Qi and Flavor:</insert> Pungent, bitter, very cold, non-toxic. <gloss>Cangqi says: Pungent, a little bitter, warm in nature, not cold. Saying it is "very cold" is a mistake.</gloss>

<insert>Indications:</insert> Masses and accumulations in the chest and abdomen, sudden illness, descends qi, breaks blood, eliminates wind-heat, dispels swelling and poisons. Its power is stronger than Yujin. <gloss>Tang Materia Medica:</gloss> Abdominal masses, blood clots, regulates menstruation, treats bruising and blood stasis, stops sudden wind-pain, and cold-gas; promotes appetite. <gloss>Daming:</gloss> Treats beatings, wards off evil, treats gas bloating and postpartum putrid blood attacking the heart. <gloss>Su Song:</gloss> Treats wind-numbness and arm pain. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Turmeric, Yujin, and <term>Shu</term> medicine are similar in shape and function. They enter the liver to treat blood within the qi, but they differ. Ancient prescriptions like the "Five Numbness Decoction" use sliced Turmeric to treat wind-cold-dampness and arm pain. Dai Yuanli’s essential formula says sliced Turmeric can enter the arms to treat pain, which shows it manages the qi within the blood.

<insert>Attached Prescriptions:</insert> <gloss>2 old, 2 new.</gloss>
**Heart pain difficult to endure:** 1 liang of Turmeric, 3 liang of cinnamon. Grind to powder, take 1 qian with vinegar decoction.
**Placenta-related abdominal pain:** <gloss>calling out, crying, vomiting milk, feces green in color, appearing like shock-convulsions, sweating all over.</gloss> 1 qian of Turmeric, myrrh, storax, frankincense (2 qian each). Grind to powder, make pills the size of foxnuts. Take one pill with <term>Uncaria rhynchophylla</term> decoction. <insert>Heji Prescription.</insert>
**Postpartum blood pain:** <gloss>Take a "square-inch ladle" dose; once the blood is discharged, it is cured.</gloss> <gloss>Jieye Chanshilu (Records of Midwifery).</gloss>
**Newly formed ringworm:** <gloss>Stir-fry to a powder and apply to the area.</gloss>

# Turmeric <note>Jianghuang</note>
<gloss>From the Materia Medica of the Tang Dynasty</gloss>

<insert>Other Names</insert> <term>Shu</term> <gloss>pronounced "shu"</gloss>, Baoding Fragrance <gloss>from the Compendium</gloss>.

<insert>Collected Explanations</insert> <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> The roots and leaves of Turmeric resemble those of *Curcuma aromatica* <note>Yujin</note>. Its flowers bloom in spring from the roots, appearing alongside the sprouts. In summer, the flowers fade, and it bears no seeds. The roots come in three colors: yellow, blue-green, and white. The processing method is the same as for *Curcuma aromatica*. The western tribes call it <term>Shu</term>. Its flavor is slightly pungent and mostly bitter, also similar to *Curcuma aromatica*, differing only in the appearance of the flowers. <gloss>Chen Zangqi says:</gloss> True Turmeric comes from old ginger plants that have been in the ground for over three years and are able to produce flowers. The flowers appear at the base of the roots just like ginger lilies. The root segments are hard, and the flavor is pungent and spicy. It is found wherever ginger is planted, though it is ultimately difficult to obtain. Some also comes from the Western regions, appearing similar to the *Yujin* drug. What Su Gong described was actually the <term>Shu</term> drug <note>Curcuma zedoaria</note> and not Turmeric. He also claimed Turmeric is <term>Shu</term> and *Curcuma aromatica* is "Foreign <term>Shu</term>." If so, there would be no distinction between the three, and they would all be called by the collective name <term>Shu</term>, implying their functions and forms are identical. However, *Curcuma aromatica* <note>Yujin</note> is bitter and cold, red in color, and primarily treats heat diseases in horses. Turmeric <note>Jianghuang</note> is pungent and warm, yellow in color. <term>Shu</term> <note>Zedoary</note> is bitter and blue-green. The three substances are different and their applications are distinct. <gloss>Li Tianming says:</gloss> Those produced in Hainan are <term>Peng'e Shu</term> <note>Zedoary</note>, while those produced south of the Yangtze River are Turmeric. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Turmeric is now found in many places across the Yangtze and Guangxi regions as well as Sichuan. The leaves are green, one to two feet long and three to four inches wide, with diagonal veins like a small red banana leaf. The flowers are reddish-white and wither by mid-autumn. In late spring, they sprout, with flowers appearing first followed by leaves. It does not bear fruit. The roots are twisted and yellow, resembling fresh ginger but rounder with segments. The roots are harvested in the eighth month, sliced, and dried in the sun. People in Sichuan use it to treat abdominal "Qi" stagnation and postpartum stagnant blood attacking the heart, with great efficacy. Local tribes eat it raw, saying it can dispel evil influences. Note that *Curcuma aromatica* <note>Yujin</note>, Turmeric <note>Jianghuang</note>, and <term>Shu</term> <note>Zedoary</note> are very similar. Su Gong could not distinguish them and treated them as one. Chen Zangqi distinguished the three by color and flavor, and claimed Turmeric grows from three-year-old ginger. In recent years, where ginger is planted extensively, Turmeric is often found; it is truly old ginger. Market sellers use this to deceive others. It is widely used in major prescriptions to treat Qi issues. There is also "Lian Jiang," which belongs to this category but is its own species. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Recently, the flat ones shaped like dried ginger are called "Sliced Turmeric" <note>Pianzi Jianghuang</note>. The round ones shaped like a cicada's belly are "Cicada-Belly Yujin." Both can be soaked in water to dye it, and the color permeates through. Although it looks like *Yujin*, the color is not as yellow.

Root <insert>Flavor and Nature</insert> Pungent and bitter, greatly cold, non-toxic. <gloss>Chen Zangqi says: It is slightly pungent and mostly bitter. Its nature is hot, not cold. The claim that it is "greatly cold" is an error.</gloss>

<insert>Primary Indications</insert> Abdominal masses and accumulations, contagious diseases <note>Zhuwu</note>, directing Qi downward, breaking up stagnant blood, removing Wind-Heat, and dissipating swellings and toxins. Its medicinal power is more intense than *Curcuma aromatica* <note>Yujin</note>. <gloss>From the Tang Materia Medica</gloss>. For abdominal masses <note>Zhengjia</note> and blood clots, regulating menstruation, treating injuries and bruises with blood stasis, stopping sudden Wind pain, cold Qi, and aiding digestion. <gloss>From Da Ming</gloss>. Treats injuries and dispels evil, treats Qi bloating, and postpartum stagnant blood attacking the heart. <gloss>From Su Song</gloss>. Treats Wind-damp numbness and arm pain. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Turmeric, *Curcuma aromatica*, and *Zedoary* are similar in form and function. This medicine enters the Liver and Spleen to treat blood within the Qi; herein lies the difference. The ancient "Five Numbness Decoction" used Sliced Turmeric to treat Wind-Cold-Dampness causing arm pain. Dai Yuanli’s *Essentials* states that Sliced Turmeric can enter the arms to treat pain, showing its ability to manage the Qi within the blood.

<insert>Attached Prescriptions</insert> <gloss>Two old, two new</gloss>
**Unbearable Heart Pain:** One ounce Turmeric, three ounces Cinnamon. Grind into powder. Take one drachm with vinegar soup.
**Abdominal Pain from Placental Issues:** <gloss>Where the infant cries, vomits milk, the stool is green as if from a fright-convulsion, and the body sweats.</gloss> One drachm Turmeric, two drachms each of Myrrh, Frankincense. Grind into powder, form into pills with honey the size of an Euryale seed. Take one pill dissolved in a decoction of Uncaria hook <note>Gouteng</note>. <insert>From the Heji Prescriptions</insert>.
**Postpartum Blood Pain:** <gloss>The pain heals as soon as the blood is expelled.</gloss> <gloss>From the Records of Midwifery</gloss>.
**Early Onset of Ringworm:** <gloss>Toast into powder and apply to the area.</gloss>

### The First Jhāna

<term>Vitakka</term> <gloss>applied thought</gloss> is like the hand; <term>vicāra</term> <gloss>sustained thought</gloss> is like the hand moving here and there. Just as when one draws a circle, the thorn held steady in the center is like <term>vitakka</term>, and the thorn circling around the outside is like <term>vicāra</term>. Thus, because it occurs with this <term>vitakka</term> and this <term>vicāra</term>, just as a tree occurs with its flowers and fruit, this <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> is called "with <term>vitakka</term> and with <term>vicāra</term>."

In the <term>Vibhanga</term> <gloss>Analysis [book of the Abhidhamma]</gloss>, however, a teaching centered on the person is given, in the manner of: "It is endowed, fully endowed with this <term>vitakka</term> and this <term>vicāra</term>." Yet the meaning in that context should be understood in just the same way.

Regarding the phrase "born of seclusion" (<term>vivekaja</term>): seclusion (<term>viveka</term>) is separation. The meaning is the departure from the hindrances. Or, "seclusion" means "secluded"; it is the mass of phenomena associated with the <term>jhāna</term> that is secluded from the hindrances. Therefore, "born of seclusion" means born from that seclusion or in that seclusion.

Regarding "rapture and happiness" (<term>pītisukha</term>): it satisfies, thus it is <term>pīti</term> <gloss>rapture</gloss>. Its characteristic is the making of affection; its function is to refresh the body and mind, or its function is to pervade; it is manifested as elation. This <term>pīti</term> is fivefold: minor rapture, momentary rapture, flooding rapture, uplifting rapture, and pervading rapture.

Of these, minor rapture is able to produce only a slight tremor of hair on the body. Momentary rapture is like flashes of lightning moment by moment. Flooding rapture breaks over the body again and again like waves on the seashore. Uplifting rapture is powerful; it is capable of lifting the body up and making it leap into the air. Indeed, the Elder Mahātissa, who lived at Puṇṇavalli, went to the courtyard of the shrine on the evening of the full moon day; seeing the moonlight and facing the Great Shrine, he thought, "At this very moment, the four assemblies are worshipping the Great Shrine," and by focusing on the Buddha as the object of meditation, he produced <term>ubbegāpīti</term> <gloss>uplifting rapture</gloss>. Like a ball struck against a plaster floor, he leapt into the air and landed right on the courtyard of the Great Shrine. Likewise, near the Girikaṇḍaka Monastery, in the village of Vattakālaka, a daughter of a family also leapt into the air due to a powerful <term>ubbegāpīti</term> based on the Buddha. It is said that her mother and father [were attending] an evening sermon...

# The First Jhāna

Applied thought <term>vitakka</term> <gloss>initial mental application</gloss> is like the hand, while sustained thought <term>vicāra</term> <gloss>sustained mental application</gloss> is like the hand moving here and there. Just as when one draws a circle, the thorn placed in the center holds the center while the thorn circling the outside traces the circumference, so too is applied thought <term>vitakka</term> the fixing of the mind, and sustained thought <term>vicāra</term> the stroking or sustained movement around it. Thus, because it occurs together with this applied thought and this sustained thought, like a tree with its flowers and fruit, this <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> is called "with applied thought and with sustained thought."

However, in the <term>Vibhanga</term> <gloss>Book of Analysis</gloss>, the teaching is presented in terms of the individual <note>personal perspective</note> using such phrases as "it is endowed with this applied thought and this sustained thought." The meaning there is to be understood in this same way.

Regarding the phrase "born of seclusion" <term>vivekaja</term>: here, seclusion <term>viveka</term> means detachment; the meaning is the departure from the hindrances. Or, "secluded" means seclusion, referring to the collection of mental states associated with the <term>jhāna</term> being secluded from the hindrances. Therefore, "born of seclusion" means that which has arisen from that seclusion or in that seclusion.

Regarding "rapture and happiness" <term>pītisukha</term>: rapture <term>pīti</term> is so called because it refreshes <note>or gladdens</note>. Its characteristic is endearing; its function is to refresh the body and mind, or to permeate them; its manifestation is elation. This rapture is of five kinds: minor rapture, momentary rapture, flooding rapture, uplifting rapture, and pervading rapture.

Of these, minor rapture is only able to cause gooseflesh on the body. Momentary rapture is like flashes of lightning moment by moment. Flooding rapture breaks over the body again and again like waves on the seashore. Uplifting rapture is powerful and capable of lifting the body up so that it leaps into the air. Thus, the Elder Mahā-Tissa, who lived at Puṇṇavallika, went to the courtyard of the shrine on a full-moon evening. Seeing the moonlight and turning toward the Great Shrine, he thought, "At this very moment, the four assemblies are worshipping the Great Shrine." By focusing on the Buddha as his object, he generated uplifting rapture and, like a ball made of painted leather struck against a plaster floor, he sprang up into the air and landed right in the courtyard of the Great Shrine. Similarly, a clanswoman in the village of Vattakālaka, near the Girikaṇḍaka Monastery, also leapt into the air due to the power of uplifting rapture based on the Buddha as her object. It is said that her parents had gone in the evening to hear the Dhamma...

He says: "Forms and so on are qualities of fire and the other elements." For it is impossible to say, "This is the quality of this [element]" regarding the indivisible elements, even if one were to claim so. Just as in various collections, because a certain element is predominant, it performs functions such as the supporting of earth and the like, so too, when there is a predominance of fire in the collections, it should be understood as a result of the manifestation of the predominant state of form and the like, and that form and the like are its qualities. They should be told: "We would agree if, in a cotton cloth <note>original: "kappāse"</note> that has an abundance of water, the scent of earth and the rest were more predominant than the scent of the cloth itself, or if the color of cold water decreased compared to the color of hot water due to an abundance of fire." Since neither of these is the case, my distinction of those supporting elements should be rejected. Just as in a single collection, even though the elements are not distinct, their form, taste, and so on are mutually different, so too should this be understood, even if there is no other distinct cause for the eye-sensitivity and the rest. But is it not the case that their own specific <term>kamma</term> <gloss>volitional action</gloss> is the very cause of their distinctness? Therefore, their distinctness comes from the distinctness of <term>kamma</term>, not from the distinctness of the elements. For if the elements were distinct, the sensitivity would not arise at all. The ancients say: "Sensitivity arises from equal elements, not from unequal ones."

629. Because they are distinct due to the distinctness of <term>kamma</term>, the eye and ear are grasp-ers of objects that have not reached them <note>i.e., non-contiguous objects</note>, because they are causes for consciousness to arise towards objects that have not clung to their own physical base. The nose, tongue, and body are grasp-ers of objects that have reached them, because they are causes for consciousness to arise towards objects that have clung to their own physical base, as well as to the base itself. However, in the commentary, because it has come into the path [of the sense organ], it is called a "reached" object. Indeed, the color of the moon and sun discs, standing at forty-two thousand <term>yojanas</term> <gloss>leagues</gloss> away, strikes the eye-sensitivity. Even though it is seen while standing far away, it is still called "reached." Being in its range, it is called the sphere of the eye-sensitivity.

Even for those cutting a tree far away, or for dyers washing cloth, the bodily action is perceived from afar. It is said that sound, through a succession of elements, strikes the ear, and then gradually goes on to be determined.

One might ask: are form and the other phenomena the qualities of the elements, such as fire? Since the elements are inseparable, it is impossible to say that this is the quality of that. However, if one were to argue that just as different elements perform their functions of supporting and so on—based on the dominance of earth and the others within various material compositions—we should likewise conclude that form and the rest are the qualities of those elements because we observe them to be more prominent in compositions where fire and the others are dominant, one must respond: we would have to accept that if moisture were dominant, the scent of the elements, such as earth, in cotton would be stronger, and that the color of cold water would be inferior to the color of hot water because of the fire dominance. Since neither of these is the case, the assumption that there is a distinction caused by their underlying elements must be abandoned. Just as the form, flavor, and other properties of elements within a single group are mutually distinct even though the elements themselves are not, so too must it be understood that the sensitive organs, such as the eye, are distinct even though there is no other cause for this variation. But what, then, is the cause of this distinction? It is their own specific <term>kamma</term> <gloss>volitional action</gloss> that is unique to each. Therefore, their distinction arises from the distinction of <term>kamma</term>, not from the distinction of the elements. If the distinction were in the elements, the sensitive faculty would not arise at all. The ancients say, "The sensitive faculty arises from similar elements, not from dissimilar ones."

629. Because these faculties are distinguished by their specific <term>kamma</term>, the eye and ear organs cognize objects they do not reach, because they serve as causes for consciousness in objects that are not in direct contact with their own physical base. The nose, tongue, and body organs cognize objects that they do reach, because they serve as causes for consciousness in objects that are in contact with their own physical base, and they themselves remain in contact with that base. In the commentary, however, an object is called "reached" if it has come into the path of the sense faculty. The color of the moon's disk and the sun's disk, even when located at a distance of forty-two thousand leagues, strikes the eye's sensitive faculty. Even though it is seen while remaining at a distance, it is still called "reached." Being in the range of the sense, it is called an object reached by the eye.

Regarding those who cut trees at a distance, or dyers washing cloth, the movement of the body is visible even from afar. However, regarding sound, it is said that it travels through a series of elements, striking the ear slowly, and only then does it become defined.

These people should be answered: we would agree if the fragrance of cotton, where earth and other elements predominate, were stronger than the fragrance of fermented liquor <note>original: "āsavassa"</note> where liquid predominates; or if the color of cold water decreased compared to the color of hot water where heat predominates. Since neither of these is the case, you should abandon your imaginative distinction regarding these supporting elements. Just as visible forms, tastes, and other qualities are different from one another even within a single group of elements despite no distinction in the elements themselves, so it should be understood that the sensitive surface of the eye <note>term: "cakkhuppasāda"</note> <gloss>the sensitive material within the eye organ capable of receiving light</gloss> and the others are different even when no other cause for distinction is present.

Is it not the case that their own unique action <note>term: "kamma"</note> <gloss>past intentional action or functional result</gloss>, which is not shared with one another, is the cause of their distinction? Therefore, their distinction comes from a distinction in action, not from a distinction in the primary elements. Indeed, if there were a distinction in the primary elements, the sensitive surface would not arise at all. For the Ancients <note>term: "porāṇā"</note> <gloss>the teachers of the old tradition</gloss> said: The sensitive surface arises from balanced elements, not from unbalanced ones.

629. Thus, among these organs distinguished by a distinction in action, the eye and the ear take objects that have not reached them <note>note: they perceive from a distance</note>, because they cause consciousness of an object that is not in contact with their own physical base. The nose, tongue, and body take objects that have reached them, because they cause consciousness only when the object is in contact with the physical base and the organ itself.

In the Commentary <note>referring to the Maha-Atthakatha</note>, however, an object is called "reached" when it has come into the range of the sense. For the color of the disks of the moon and sun, situated forty-two thousand leagues away, strikes the sensitive surface of the eye. Although perceived while standing at a distance, it is indeed called reached. Because it is within the eye's range, the eye is said to have a reached object as its field.

When people are cutting a tree or when washermen are washing clothes at a distance, the movement of the body is seen from afar. But the sound, it is said, strikes the ear through a succession of elements and gradually reaches its determination.

<summary>Buddhaghosa discusses the relationship between primary elements and sensory qualities, arguing that sense organs differ due to past karma rather than elemental composition. He also classifies the senses into those that perceive distant objects and those requiring direct contact.</summary>
